title: Economic potential of generative AI
content:
- **Page relevance**
  - Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases.
  - Provides:
    - quantified value estimates for generative AI use cases
    - named business functions and use cases
    - adoption, productivity, and ROI-style findings
    - workflow / agentic-style operating patterns such as copilots, virtual experts, virtual collaborators, AI assistants, chatbots, code acceleration
    - governance, risk, quality-control, privacy, and regulatory obligations
    - failure modes such as hallucination, bias, plagiarism, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, misinformation, deepfakes, and explainability limits

- **Quantitative estimates and value sizing**
  - “generative AI could add the equivalent of **$2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion annually** across the **63 use cases** we analyzed”
  - “This would increase the impact of all artificial intelligence by **15 to 40 percent**”
  - “This estimate would roughly **double** if we include the impact of embedding generative AI into software that is currently used for other tasks beyond those use cases”
  - “Across **16 business functions**, we examined **63 use cases**”
  - “About **75 percent** of the value that generative AI use cases could deliver falls across four areas: **Customer operations, marketing and sales, software engineering, and R&D**”
  - “Banking, high tech, and life sciences are among the industries that could see the biggest impact as a percentage of their revenues”
  - “Across the banking industry, for example, the technology could deliver value equal to an additional **$200 billion to $340 billion annually** if the use cases were fully implemented”
  - “In retail and consumer packaged goods, the potential impact is also significant at **$400 billion to $660 billion a year**”
  - “Current generative AI and other technologies have the potential to automate work activities that absorb **60 to 70 percent of employees’ time today**”
  - “our updated adoption scenarios … lead to estimates that **half of today’s work activities could be automated between 2030 and 2060, with a midpoint in 2045**, or roughly a decade earlier than in our previous estimates”
  - “Generative AI could enable labor productivity growth of **0.1 to 0.6 percent annually through 2040**”
  - “Combining generative AI with all other technologies, work automation could add **0.5 to 3.4 percentage points annually** to productivity growth”
  - “Across the **63 use cases** we analyzed, generative AI has the potential to generate **$2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion** in value across industries”
  - “the total economic benefits of generative AI … amounts to **$6.1 trillion to $7.9 trillion annually**”
  - “the potential value generative AI can deliver in function-specific use cases … could drive value across an entire organization by revolutionizing internal knowledge management systems”
  - “knowledge workers spent about **a fifth of their time, or one day each work week**, searching for and gathering information”
  - “In 2012, the McKinsey Global Institute (MGI) estimated that knowledge workers spent about a fifth of their time, or one day each work week, searching for and gathering information”
  - “for retail and consumer packaged goods (CPG) … productivity by **1.2 to 2.0 percent of annual revenues**, or an additional **$400 billion to $660 billion**”
  - “banking … increased productivity of **2.8 to 4.7 percent of the industry’s annual revenues**, or an additional **$200 billion to $340 billion**”
  - “pharmaceutical and medical-product industries … **2.6 to 4.5 percent of annual revenues** … or **$60 billion to $110 billion annually**”

- **Named functions, use cases, and specific workflow patterns**
  - **Customer operations**
    - “support interactions with customers”
    - “digital self-service”
    - “enhancing and augmenting agent skills”
    - “customer self-service”
    - “Resolution during initial contact”
    - “Reduced response time”
    - “Increased sales”
    - “quality assurance and coaching”
    - “customer care functions”
    - “customer service”
    - “call-center agents”
    - “wealth management financial advisers”
    - “always-on, deep technical support”
    - “customer-facing chatbots”
    - “service professionals could rapidly access all relevant information”
  - **Marketing and sales**
    - “generate creative content for marketing and sales”
    - “personalized messages tailored to individual customer interests, preferences, and behaviors”
    - “producing first drafts of brand advertising, headlines, slogans, social media posts, and product descriptions”
    - “Efficient and effective content creation”
    - “Enhanced use of data”
    - “SEO optimization”
    - “Product discovery and search personalization”
    - “Increase probability of sale”
    - “Improve lead development”
    - “personalized marketing campaigns through a chatbot”
    - “cross-sell and upsell”
    - “A/B testing”
  - **Software engineering**
    - “draft computer code based on natural-language prompts”
    - “pair programming”
    - “augmented coding”
    - “generate code when given a natural-language prompt describing what that code should do”
    - “generating initial code drafts”
    - “code correction and refactoring”
    - “root-cause analysis”
    - “generating new system designs”
    - “automatic translations and no- and low-code tools”
    - “generate, prioritize, run, and review different code tests”
    - “integrated with OpenAI’s GPT-4”
    - “GitHub Copilot”
    - “Replit”
  - **R&D / product development**
    - “Product R&D: Reducing research and design time, improving simulation and testing”
    - “generative design”
    - “generate candidate molecules”
    - “design small-molecule therapeutics”
    - “Enhanced design”
    - “Improved product testing and quality”
    - “deep learning surrogates”
    - “accelerate the testing of designs proposed by generative AI”
    - “lead identification”
    - “Improve automation of preliminary screening”
    - “Enhance indication finding”
  - **Knowledge management / internal expert systems**
    - “revolutionizing internal knowledge management systems”
    - “retrieve stored internal knowledge”
    - “continuing dialogue”
    - “virtual expertise”
  - **Banking-specific**
    - “required reporting”
    - “monitoring regulatory developments”
    - “collecting data”
    - “credit risk scoring”
    - “model documentation”
    - “identify missing documentation”
    - “scan relevant regulatory updates to create alerts”
  - **Retail / CPG-specific**
    - “tracking or canceling an order”
    - “offering discounts”
    - “upselling”
    - “packaging designs from scratch”
    - “generate variations on an existing design”
    - “text-to-video generation”
  - **Pharma / medical products**
    - “preliminary screening of chemicals”
    - “lead optimization”
    - “identification and prioritization of new indications”
    - “quantify clinical events, establish relationships, and measure the similarity”
    - “high success rates in clinical trials”
    - “Phase 3 trials”

- **Adoption / ROI / productivity findings**
  - **Customer operations**
    - “at one company with **5,000 customer service agents**”
    - “increased issue resolution by **14 percent an hour**”
    - “reduced the time spent handling an issue by **9 percent**”
    - “reduced agent attrition and requests to speak to a manager by **25 percent**”
    - “productivity and quality of service improved most among less-experienced agents”
    - “the AI assistant did not increase—and sometimes decreased—the productivity and quality metrics of more highly skilled agents”
    - “We estimate that applying generative AI to customer care functions could increase productivity at a value ranging from **30 to 45 percent of current function costs**”
    - “roughly half of customer contacts made by banking, telecommunications, and utilities companies in North America are already handled by machines, including but not exclusively AI”
    - “generative AI could further reduce the volume of human-serviced contacts by **up to 50 percent**, depending on a company’s existing level of automation”
  - **Marketing**
    - “We estimate that generative AI could increase the productivity of the marketing function with a value between **5 and 15 percent of total marketing spending**”
  - **Sales**
    - “implementing generative AI could increase sales productivity by approximately **3 to 5 percent of current global sales expenditures**”
  - **Software engineering**
    - “the direct impact of AI on the productivity of software engineering could range from **20 to 45 percent of current annual spending on the function**”
    - “One study found that software developers using Microsoft’s GitHub Copilot completed tasks **56 percent faster** than those not using the tool”
    - “Replit, used by **more than 20 million coders**”
  - **R&D**
    - “generative AI could deliver productivity with a value ranging from **10 to 15 percent of overall R&D costs**”
    - “lead identification … can take several months even with ‘traditional’ deep learning techniques”
    - “Foundation models and generative AI can enable organizations to complete this step in **a matter of weeks**”
    - “Pharma companies that have used this approach have reported high success rates in clinical trials for the top five indications recommended by a foundation model for a tested drug”
    - “These drugs [have] progress[ed] smoothly into Phase 3 trials, significantly accelerating the drug development process”
  - **Industry / sector**
    - “For example, our analysis estimates generative AI could contribute roughly **$310 billion** in additional value for the retail industry (including auto dealerships)”
    - “the bulk of potential value in high tech comes from generative AI’s ability to increase the speed and efficiency of software development”

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors and operating patterns**
  - “Generative AI has the potential to revolutionize the entire customer operations function”
  - “The technology has already gained traction in customer service because of its ability to automate interactions with customers using natural language”
  - “AI assistance helped less-experienced agents communicate using techniques similar to those of their higher-skilled counterparts”
  - “AI assistant did not increase—and sometimes decreased—the productivity and quality metrics of more highly skilled agents”
  - “significant human oversight is required for conceptual and strategic thinking specific to each company’s needs”
  - “retail and CPG companies will need to strategically keep humans in the loop”
  - “ensure security and privacy are top considerations for any implementation”
  - “Companies will need to institute new quality checks for processes previously handled by humans”
  - “perform more-detailed quality checks on AI-assisted processes”
  - “intended level of work automation”
    - “AI agents integrated through APIs could act nearly autonomously or as copilots, giving real-time suggestions to agents during customer interactions”
  - “One European bank has leveraged generative AI to develop an environmental, social, and governance (ESG) virtual expert”
  - “The model answers complex questions based on a prompt, identifying the source of each answer and extracting information from pictures and tables”
  - “Morgan Stanley is building an AI assistant using GPT-4, with the aim of helping tens of thousands of wealth managers quickly find and synthesize answers from a massive internal knowledge base”
  - “The model combines search and content creation so wealth managers can find and tailor information for any client at any moment”
  - “Service professionals could rapidly access all relevant information such as product guides and policies to instantaneously address customer requests”
  - “generative AI tools are useful for software development in four broad categories”
    - “draft code based on context via input code or natural language”
    - “automatically generate, prioritize, run, and review different code tests”
    - “natural-language translation capabilities can optimize the integration and migration of legacy frameworks”
    - “review code to identify defects and inefficiencies in computing”
  - “In addition to the productivity gains … generative design can also enable improvements in the designs themselves”
  - “Using generative AI in generative design can produce a higher-quality product”

- **Governance, risk, compliance, privacy, and obligations**
  - “Introducing generative AI to marketing functions requires careful consideration”
  - “mathematical models trained on publicly available data without sufficient safeguards against plagiarism, copyright violations, and branding recognition risks infringing on intellectual property rights”
  - “A virtual try-on application may produce biased representations of certain demographics because of limited or biased training data”
  - “External inference”
    - “Generative AI has increased the need to understand whether generated content is based on fact or inference, requiring a new level of quality control”
  - “Adversarial attacks”
    - “Foundation models are a prime target for attack by hackers and other bad actors”
    - “increasing the variety of potential security vulnerabilities and privacy risks”
  - “The level of regulation for different processes”
    - “These vary from unregulated processes such as customer service to heavily regulated processes such as credit risk scoring”
  - “Data constraints”
    - “there would need to be limits on identifiable details for customers and other internal data”
  - “The need for a human in the loop”
    - “Companies may need to implement new quality checks on processes that shift from humans to generative AI”
    - “The increasing need to verify whether generated content is based on fact or inference elevates the need for a new level of quality control”
  - “Explainability”
    - “A lack of transparency into the origins of generated content and traceability of root data could make it difficult to update models and scan them for potential risks”
    - “a generative AI solution for synthesizing scientific literature may not be able to point to the specific articles or quotes that led it to infer that a new treatment is very popular among physicians”
    - “Systems need to be designed to point to specific articles or data sources, and then do human-in-the-loop checking”
  - “Privacy considerations”
    - “Generative AI’s use of clinical images and medical records could increase the risk that protected health information will leak, potentially violating regulations that require pharma companies to protect patient privacy”
  - “Security”
    - “Generative AI may be used by bad actors to accelerate the sophistication and speed of cyberattacks”
    - “prompt injection”
  - “Reliability”
    - “Models can produce different answers to the same prompts, impeding the user’s ability to assess the accuracy and reliability of outputs”
  - “Organizational impact”
    - “Generative AI may significantly affect the workforce, and the impact on specific groups and local communities could be disproportionately negative”
  - “Social and environmental impact”
    - “training one large language model can emit about **315 tons of carbon dioxide**”
  - “Fairness”
    - “Models may generate algorithmic bias due to imperfect training data or decisions made by the engineers developing the models”
  - “Intellectual property (IP)”
    - “Training data and model outputs can generate significant IP risks, including infringing on copyrighted, trademarked, patented, or otherwise legally protected materials”
    - “organizations will need to understand what data went into training and how it’s used in tool outputs”
  - “disinformation, deepfakes, and hate speech”
  - “hallucinate”
    - “generate responses that are obviously incorrect or inappropriate for the context”

- **Failure modes and limitations explicitly stated**
  - “plagiarism”
  - “copyright violations”
  - “branding recognition risks”
  - “biased representations”
  - “External inference”
  - “Adversarial attacks”
  - “privacy risks”
  - “hallucinate”
  - “different answers to the same prompts”
  - “lack of transparency”
  - “traceability of root data”
  - “prompt injection”
  - “malicious content such as disinformation, deepfakes, and hate speech”
  - “obviously incorrect or inappropriate for the context”
  - “decrease[d] the productivity and quality metrics of more highly skilled agents”
  - “could not fully account for … knock-on effects”
  - “did not account for the increase in application quality”
  - “did not attempt to estimate the technology’s potential to create entirely novel product categories”
  - “foundation models lack the capabilities to help design products across all industries”

- **Named companies / examples**
  - ChatGPT
  - GitHub Copilot
  - Stable Diffusion
  - OpenAI
  - GPT-4
  - Anthropic
  - Claude
  - Google
  - Search Generative Experience
  - PaLM 2
  - Bard
  - Stitch Fix
  - DALL·E
  - Morgan Stanley
  - European bank
  - Entos
  - Replit
  - Microsoft
  - McKinsey Global Institute

- **Explicit absence / scope limitations stated on the page**
  - “Our estimates are based on the structure of the global economy in 2022 and do not consider the value generative AI could create if it produced entirely new product or service categories”
  - “Our analysis captures only the direct impact generative AI might have on the productivity of customer operations”
  - “Our analysis of the potential use of generative AI in marketing doesn’t account for knock-on effects beyond the direct impacts on productivity”
  - “Our analysis did not account for the increase in application quality and the resulting boost in productivity that generative AI could bring by improving code or enhancing IT architecture”
  - “While we have estimated the potential direct impacts of generative AI on the R&D function, we did not attempt to estimate the technology’s potential to create entirely novel product categories”
  - “the full realization of the technology’s benefits will take time”
  - “leaders in business and society still have considerable challenges to address”
description: Generative AI’s impact on productivity could add trillions of dollars in value to the global economy—and the era is just beginning.

title: The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation
content:
- **Page relevance**
  - Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases.
  - Contains enterprise AI adoption, use-case patterns, agentic AI, workflow redesign, governance/risk, and performance/ROI findings.

- **Quantitative estimates and adoption findings**
  - “Nearly two-thirds of respondents say their organizations have not yet begun scaling AI across the enterprise.”
  - “Sixty-two percent of survey respondents say their organizations are at least experimenting with AI agents.”
  - “88 percent report regular AI use in at least one business function, compared with 78 percent a year ago.”
  - “Approximately one-third” report that their companies have begun to scale their AI programs.
  - “Twenty-three percent of respondents report their organizations are scaling an agentic AI system somewhere in their enterprises.”
  - “An additional 39 percent say they have begun experimenting with AI agents.”
  - “In any given business function, no more than 10 percent of respondents say their organizations are scaling AI agents.”
  - “More than two-thirds of respondents now say their organizations are using AI in more than one function, and half report using AI in three or more functions.”
  - “Nearly half of respondents from companies with more than $5 billion in revenue have reached the scaling phase, compared with 29 percent of those with less than $100 million in revenues.”
  - “Thirty-nine percent of respondents attribute any level of EBIT impact to AI.”
  - “Most of those respondents say that less than 5 percent of their organization’s EBIT is attributable to AI use.”
  - “A majority say that their organizations’ use of AI has improved innovation, and nearly half report improvement in customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation.”
  - “Thirty-two percent predict an overall reduction of 3 percent or more, and 13 percent predict an increase of that magnitude.”
  - “Across business functions, a median of 17 percent of respondents report declines in functions’ workforce size in the past year as a result of AI use, but a median of 30 percent expect a decrease in the next year.”
  - “51 percent of respondents from organizations using AI say their organizations have seen at least one instance of a negative consequence.”
  - “Nearly one-third of all respondents reporting consequences stemming from AI inaccuracy.”
  - “Back in 2022, respondents reported acting to manage an average of two AI-related risks, compared with four risks today.”
  - “More than one-third of high performers say their organizations are committing more than 20 percent of their digital budgets to AI technologies.”
  - “About three-quarters of high performers say their organizations are scaling or have scaled AI, compared with one-third of other organizations.”
  - “AI high performers are more than three times more likely than others are to say their organization intends to use AI to bring about transformative change to their businesses.”
  - “AI high performers are nearly three times as likely as others are to say their organizations have fundamentally redesigned individual workflows.”
  - “In most business functions, AI high performers are at least three times more likely than their peers to report that they are scaling their use of agents.”
  - “High performers are three times more likely than their peers to strongly agree that senior leaders at their organizations demonstrate ownership of and commitment to their AI initiatives.”
  - “AI high performers, who say their organizations have deployed twice as many AI use cases as others have, are more likely than others to report negative consequences.”
  - “Thirty-eight percent of respondents say they work for organizations with more than $1 billion in annual revenues.”
  - Survey field period: “June 25 to July 29, 2025”
  - Sample size: “1,993 participants”
  - Coverage: “105 nations”

- **Named functions / use cases**
  - “IT and knowledge management” are the business functions where agent use is most commonly reported.
  - Agentic use cases named:
    - “service-desk management in IT”
    - “deep research in knowledge management”
  - Functions most often reported as using AI:
    - “IT”
    - “marketing and sales”
    - “knowledge management”
  - Individual use cases within business functions:
    - “capture information”
    - “processing and delivering it, such as through a conversational interface”
    - “content support for marketing strategy, including drafting, generating ideas, and presenting knowledge for creating marketing strategies”
    - “contact-center or customer service automation”
  - Cost-benefit use cases:
    - “software engineering”
    - “manufacturing”
    - “IT”
  - Revenue-increase use cases:
    - “marketing and sales”
    - “strategy and corporate finance”
    - “product and service development”
  - AI-agent sectors most widely reported:
    - “technology”
    - “media and telecommunications”
    - “healthcare”

- **Adoption / ROI / value findings**
  - “Use-case-level cost and revenue benefits”
  - “64 percent say that AI is enabling their innovation.”
  - “39 percent report EBIT impact at the enterprise level.”
  - “Respondents who attribute EBIT impact of 5 percent or more to AI use and say their organization has seen ‘significant’ value from AI use—our definition of AI high performers, representing about 6 percent of respondents…”
  - High performers report:
    - “pushing for transformative innovation via AI”
    - “redesigning workflows”
    - “scaling faster”
    - “implementing best practices for transformation”
    - “investing more”
  - “Efficiency gains” are the objective for “80 percent of respondents.”
  - High performers are more likely to have set:
    - “growth”
    - “innovation”
    as objectives of AI efforts.
  - Qualitative enterprise-level benefits associated with growth/innovation use:
    - “improved customer satisfaction”
    - “competitive differentiation”
    - “profitability”
    - “revenue growth”
    - “change in market share”

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors**
  - “Redesigning workflows is a key success factor.”
  - “Most are redesigning workflows.”
  - “Intentional redesigning of workflows has one of the strongest contributions to achieving meaningful business impact of all the factors tested.”
  - High performers are more likely to have:
    - “senior leaders … demonstrate ownership of and commitment to their AI initiatives”
    - “senior leaders are actively engaged in driving AI adoption, including role modeling the use of AI”
    - “defined processes to determine how and when model outputs need human validation to ensure accuracy”
    - “an agile product delivery organization, or an enterprise-wide agile organization with well-defined delivery processes”
    - “robust talent strategies”
    - “technology and data infrastructure”
    - “embedding AI into business processes”
    - “tracking KPIs for AI solutions”
  - The management practices span “six dimensions essential to capturing value from AI: strategy, talent, operating model, technology, data, and adoption and scaling.”
  - “All of the management practices we tested correlate positively with value attributable to AI.”

- **Governance / risk obligations**
  - Risks with increased mitigation efforts:
    - “personal and individual privacy”
    - “explainability”
    - “organizational reputation”
    - “regulatory compliance”
  - “Inaccuracy is one of two risks that most respondents say their organizations are working to mitigate.”
  - “The second-most-commonly-reported risk—explainability—is not among the most commonly mitigated.”
  - High performers report more negative consequences, particularly:
    - “intellectual property infringement”
    - “regulatory compliance”
  - High performers “also try to protect against a larger number of risks.”

- **Failure modes / negative consequences**
  - “Most organizations have not yet embedded them deeply enough into their workflows and processes to realize material enterprise-level benefits.”
  - “The majority are still in the experimenting or piloting stages.”
  - “Most of those who are scaling agents say they’re only doing so in one or two functions.”
  - “Use of agents is not yet widespread.”
  - “No more than 10 percent” scaling AI agents in any given business function.
  - “Meaningful enterprise-wide bottom-line impact from the use of AI continues to be rare.”
  - “AI use has not yet significantly affected enterprise-wide EBIT.”
  - “Respondents are more likely to say their organizations are mitigating each of the risks they have experienced consequences from.”
  - “51 percent” have seen “at least one instance of a negative consequence.”
  - “Nearly one-third” report consequences stemming from “AI inaccuracy.”
  - High performers report more negative consequences “particularly related to intellectual property infringement and regulatory compliance.”
  - “Explainability” is a risk that is commonly reported but “not among the most commonly mitigated.”

- **Workforce impact findings**
  - “32 percent expect decreases, 43 percent no change, and 13 percent increases” in organizational workforce size in the coming year.
  - “A plurality of respondents observed little to no change in the number of employees due to their organization’s use of AI in the past year.”
  - “In most functions, fewer than 20 percent of respondents report decreases of 3 percent or more.”
  - “Smaller shares say their organization’s AI use led them to add head count within functions.”
  - “Most respondents—and an even larger share from larger companies—note that their organizations hired for AI-related roles over the past year.”
  - “Software engineers and data engineers are the most in demand.”

- **Industry / function-specific adoption detail**
  - “In every industry besides the technology sector” AI use rose meaningfully since the previous survey.
  - “Media and telecommunications and insurance are just as likely as those in technology to report AI use.”
  - “Throughout eight years of AI research, we have consistently seen IT and marketing and sales as the business functions that respondents most often say are using AI.”
  - “Knowledge management is now also one of the functions with the most reported AI use.”
description: In this 2025 edition of the annual McKinsey Global Survey on AI, we look at the current trends that are driving real value from artificial intelligence.

title: Seizing the agentic AI advantage - McKinsey
content:
- **Page relevance:** Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases because it provides explicit evidence on:
  - adoption versus impact
  - horizontal versus vertical use cases
  - workflow reinvention
  - named enterprise functions and processes
  - quantitative productivity / savings / impact estimates
  - governance, risk, and architecture requirements
  - failure modes and barriers to scaling

- **At a glance / headline findings**
  - “Nearly eight in ten companies report using gen AI—yet just as many report no significant bottom-line impact.”
  - “The heart of this paradox is an imbalance between ‘horizontal’ (enterprise-wide) copilots and chatbots—which have scaled quickly but deliver diffuse, hard-to-measure gains—and more transformative ‘vertical’ (function-specific) use cases—about 90 percent of which remain stuck in pilot mode.”
  - “AI agents offer a way to break out of the gen AI paradox.”
  - “Agents have the potential to automate complex business processes—combining autonomy, planning, memory, and integration—to shift gen AI from a reactive tool to a proactive, goal-driven virtual collaborator.”
  - “This shift enables far more than efficiency. Agents supercharge operational agility and create new revenue opportunities.”
  - “Unlocking the full potential of agentic AI requires more than plugging agents into existing workflows. It calls for reimagining those workflows from the ground up—with agents at the core.”

- **Adoption, maturity, ROI, and impact findings**
  - “Nearly eight in ten companies have deployed gen AI in some form, but roughly the same percentage report no material impact on earnings.”
  - “More than 80 percent of companies still report no material contribution to earnings from their gen AI initiatives.”
  - “Only 1 percent of enterprises we surveyed view their gen AI strategies as mature.”
  - “More than 78 percent of companies are now using gen AI in at least one business function (up from 55 percent a year earlier).”
  - “Nearly 70 percent of Fortune 500 companies, for example, use Microsoft 365 Copilot.”
  - “Fewer than 10 percent of use cases deployed ever make it past the pilot stage, according to McKinsey research.”
  - “From 2018 to 2022, for example, AI adoption remained relatively stagnant, with about 50 percent of companies deploying the technology in just one business function.”
  - “The technology’s estimated value potential was already immense—between $11 trillion and $18 trillion globally—mainly in the fields of marketing ..., sales ..., and supply chain ...”
  - “McKinsey estimates that the technology has the potential to unlock $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion in additional value on top of the value potential of traditional analytical AI.”
  - “Annual run costs typically represent 10 to 20 percent of initial build costs” for traditional IT systems.
  - “Gen AI solutions, especially at scale, can incur recurring costs that exceed the initial build investment.”

- **Named functions / use cases / business areas explicitly mentioned**
  - **Marketing**
    - “personalized email targeting”
    - “customer segmentation”
  - **Sales**
    - “lead scoring”
  - **Supply chain**
    - “inventory optimization”
    - “demand forecasting”
    - “autonomous orchestration layer across sourcing, warehousing, and distribution operations”
    - “monitoring disruptions”
    - “rerouting operations”
    - “supply chain planning system”
    - “warehouse management system”
    - “weather forecasts”
    - “supplier feeds”
    - “demand signals”
    - “forecast demand”
    - “identify risks, such as delays or disruptions”
    - “dynamically replan transport and inventory flows”
    - “selecting the optimal transport mode based on cost, lead time, and environmental impact”
    - “reallocate stock across warehouses”
    - “negotiate directly with external systems”
    - “escalate decisions requiring strategic input”
  - **E-commerce**
    - “embedded into online stores or apps”
    - “proactively analyze user behavior, cart content, and context”
    - “real-time upselling and cross-selling offers”
  - **Finance**
    - “help customers discover suitable financial products such as loans, insurance plans, or investment portfolios”
    - “tailored guidance based on financial profiles, life events, and user behavior”
    - “credit-risk memos”
    - “credit decisions”
    - “regulatory requirements”
  - **Industrial companies**
    - “embedded in connected products or equipment”
    - “monitor usage”
    - “detect performance thresholds”
    - “autonomously unlock features”
    - “trigger maintenance actions”
    - “pay-per-use, subscription, or performance-based models of creating revenue”
  - **Service organizations**
    - “encapsulate internal expertise—legal reasoning, tax interpretation, and procurement best practices—into AI agents offered as software-as-a-service tools or APIs”

title: Deloitte’s State of Generative AI in the Enterprise
content:
- **Relevance:** Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases. The page contains quantitative adoption, ROI, workflow/agentic AI, governance/risk, and failure-mode evidence across enterprise GenAI initiatives.

- **Report / survey context**
  - “Quarter four report”
  - “January 2025”
  - Deloitte’s fourth quarterly survey conducted “July – September 2024”
  - N (Total leader survey responses) = **2,773**
  - Survey fields: “2,773 director- to C-suite-level respondents across six industries and 14 countries”
  - Industries included:
    - consumer
    - energy, resources and industrials
    - financial services
    - life sciences and health care
    - technology, media and telecom
    - government and public services
  - The survey data was augmented by “15 interviews with C-suite executives and AI and data science leaders at large organizations across a range of industries”
  - 14 countries represented:
    - Australia (100 respondents)
    - Brazil (115 respondents)
    - Canada (175 respondents)
    - France (130 respondents)
    - Germany (150 respondents)
    - India (200 respondents)
    - Italy (75 respondents)
    - Japan (100 respondents)
    - Mexico (100 respondents)
    - the Netherlands (50 respondents)
    - Singapore (75 respondents)
    - Spain (100 respondents)
    - the United Kingdom (200 respondents)
    - the United States (1,203 respondents)

- **Definitions / conceptual framing**
  - “Generative AI is an evolving area of artificial intelligence and refers to AI that in response to a query—a prompt—can create new text, images, video and other assets.”
  - GenAI systems “can interact with humans” and are built/trained on datasets ranging “from small language models (SLMs) to large language models (LLMs).”
  - “Emerging AI agents are software systems that can complete complex tasks and meet objectives with little or no human intervention.”
  - Agents “have the agency to act independently, planning and executing actions to achieve a specified goal.”
  - “The vision for agentic AI is that autonomous AI agents will be able to execute assigned tasks consistently and reliably by acquiring and processing multimodal data, using various tools to complete tasks, and coordinating with other AI agents—all while remembering what they’ve done in the past and learning from their experience.”

- **High-level findings relevant to ranking use cases**
  - “The IT function is most mature; cybersecurity, operations, marketing and customer service are also showing strong adoption and results.”
  - “Organizations reporting higher ROI for their most scaled initiatives are broadly further along in their GenAI journeys.”
  - “Beyond the IT function, organizations tend to focus their deepest GenAI deployments on parts of the business uniquely critical to success in their industries.”
  - Examples of business-specific use cases explicitly listed:
    - “Brand promotion and integrated business planning in the consumer products industry”
    - “Predictive maintenance for physical assets in the energy industry”
    - “Drug discovery and clinical trial tracking in the pharmaceutical industry”
    - “Cybersecurity and portfolio management in the financial services industry”
    - “Sales enablement, chip development and improved search in the technology industry”
    - “Archive management and music source separation in the media and entertainment industry”

- **Adoption / maturity findings**
  - “Access to GenAI is still largely limited to less than 40% of the workforce.”
  - “For most organizations, fewer than 60% of workers who have access to GenAI actually use it on a daily basis.”
  - “Over two-thirds of respondents said that 30% or fewer of their current experiments will be fully scaled in the next three to six months.”
  - “The lion’s share of organizations are currently pursuing 20 or fewer GenAI experiments or proofs of concept (POCs) and expect to fully scale 10%–30% of those experiments in the next three to six months.”
  - “larger numbers of experiments” are being conducted by organizations that are:
    - large
    - advanced in their use of AI
    - and/or operating in key industries of technology, media and telecommunications; life sciences and health care; or financial services
  - “The adoption rate for customized, open-source and/or proprietary large language models (LLMs) remains limited at 20%–25% of those surveyed.”
  - “The vast majority of respondents (78%) reported they expect to increase their overall AI spending in the next fiscal year”
  - “the percentage of organizations investing 20%–39% of their overall AI budget on GenAI climbed by 12 points”
  - “the percentage of organizations investing less than 20% of their AI budget on GenAI fell by 6 points”
  - C-suite perception gap:
    - “21% of C-suite survey respondents reported they feel GenAI is already transforming their organization, compared to only 8% of non-C-suite respondents.”
    - “Sixty percent of non-C-suite respondents believe it will take 12 months or more to overcome scaling barriers, compared to only 47% of C-suite respondents.”

- **Barriers / governance / risk / compliance**
  - “Regulatory uncertainty and risk management have risen in organizations’ lists of concerns to address.”
  - “Levels of trust in GenAI are still moderate for the majority of organizations.”
  - “With increased customization and accuracy of models—combined with a focus on better governance—adoption of GenAI is becoming more established.”
  - “Regulatory compliance has emerged from the pack to become the top barrier holding organizations back from developing and deploying GenAI tools and applications.”
  - Figure 2 top barriers to developing and deploying GenAI:
    - “Worries about complying with regulations” = **38%**
    - “Difficulty managing risks” = **36%**
    - “Lack of an adoption strategy” = **27%**
    - “Difficulty identifying use cases” = **27%**
    - “Trouble choosing the right technologies” = **26%**
    - “Implementation challenges” = **26%**
    - “Lack of technical talent and skills” = **24%**
    - “Lack of a governance model” = **22%**
    - “Cultural resistance from employees” = **17%**
    - “Not having the right comp. infrastructure / data” = **17%**
    - “Lack of executive commitment and/or funding” = **14%**
  - “Governments today face the monumental task of regulating a technology whose capabilities are still taking shape.”
  - “This highlights respondents’ unease about which use cases will be acceptable, and to what extent their organizations will be held accountable for GenAI-related problems.”
  - In future adoption barriers:
    - “mistakes / errors with real-world consequences” = **35%**
    - “not achieving expected value” = **34%**
    - “shortage of high-quality data” = **30%**
    - “general loss of trust due to bias, hallucinations and inaccuracies” = **29%**
    - “Intellectual property issues” = **25%**
    - “Concerns over energy usage / environmental concerns” = **20%**
    - “Rising cost of building and operating models / tools / applications” = **13%**
    - “AI sovereignty issues” = **12%**
  - Time to resolve GenAI challenges:
    - “Implementing a governance strategy”
      - Less than 1 year = **29%**
      - 1 to 2 years = **52%**
      - More than 2 years = **17%**
    - “Achieving ROI”
      - Less than 1 year = **26%**
      - 1 to 2 years = **55%**
      - More than 2 years = **15%**
    - “Acquiring talent”
      - Less than 1 year = **37%**
      - 1 to 2 years = **51%**
      - More than 2 years = **9%**
    - “Addressing data challenges”
      - Less than 1 year = **39%**
      - 1 to 2 years = **49%**
      - More than 2 years = **9%**
    - “Overcoming scaling barriers”
      - Less than 1 year = **40%**
      - 1 to 2 years = **51%**
      - More than 2 years = **8%**
    - “Training workers”
      - Less than 1 year = **42%**
      - 1 to 2 years = **48%**
      - More than 2 years = **8%**
    - “Managing trust issues”
      - Less than 1 year = **44%**
      - 1 to 2 years = **48%**
      - More than 2 years = **7%**
  - “70% of respondents said their organizations will need at least 12 months to resolve the challenges related to surpassing or achieving their expected ROI from GenAI.”
  - “76% reported their organizations will wait at least 12 months before reducing investment in a GenAI initiative that is not meeting its value targets.”
  - “The key barriers currently facing GenAI—such as regulatory uncertainty, inadequate risk management, data deficiencies, and workforce / talent issues—still apply and are arguably even more important and challenging due to the increased complexity of agentic AI systems.”
  - The page explicitly recommends:
    - “Map out the risks associated with autonomous agents and create mitigation plans.”
    - “Start with low-risk use cases that use noncritical data—with human oversight as a backup.”
    - These steps “can help test and build the data management, cybersecurity and governance capabilities necessary for safe agentic AI applications.”
  - Governance / leadership obligations stated:
    - “Chief executive officers should show top-down support for GenAI, be the champions for governance and risk initiatives, and foster an environment of trust and transparency.”
    - “Chief information officers, chief technology officers and chief data officers should sharpen their focus on identifying and overcoming the barriers to large-scale GenAI deployment within their domains.”
    - “Chief financial officers should ensure responsible spending without stifling innovation.”
    - “chief human resource officers should promote training, reskilling and other human capital investments.”
  - C-suite considerations:
    - “ensure the organization stays aligned”
    - “manage organizational expectations”
    - “show patience in the face of uncertainty”

- **Quantitative adoption / workflow findings**
  - “The C-suite sees things differently.”
  - “The IT function came out on top (28%).”
  - Other most advanced scaled initiative functions:
    - Operations = **11%**
    - Marketing = **10%**
    - Customer service = **8%**
    - Cybersecurity = **8%**
    - Product development = **6%**
    - R&D = **7%**
    - Sales = **5%**
    - Strategy = **4%**
    - Supply chain = **5%**
    - Finance = **4%**
    - HR = **2%**
    - Manufacturing = **2%**
    - Legal, risk, compliance = **1%**
  - “GenAI initiatives are most advanced within these functions”
  - Industry top three most advanced scaled GenAI initiatives:
    - Consumer:
      - IT **96%**
      - Operations **3%**
    - Energy, resources & industrial:
      - IT **34%**
      - Product dev **17%**
      - Cybersecurity **12%**
    - Financial services:
      - IT **23%**
      - R&D **21%**
      - Operations **11%**
    - Life sciences & health care:
      - IT **21%**
      - Cybersecurity **14%**
      - Finance **13%**
    - Tech, media & telecom:
      - Operations **23%**
      - IT **17%**
      - Strategy **11%**
    - Government:
      - IT **20%**
      - Marketing **20%**
      - Customer service **12%**

- **Benefits targeted / achieved**
  - “Improved efficiency and productivity” continue to be the most commonly sought benefits from GenAI.
  - “many organizations (40%) reported they are already achieving their expected benefits in this area to a large or very large extent.”
  - Higher success in strategic benefit areas:
    - “new ideas and insights” = **46%**
    - “innovation and growth” = **45%**
  - “46% of respondents (seeking the benefit) reported that they are uncovering new ideas and insights with GenAI.”
  - Benefit categories listed in figure:
    - Detect fraud and manage risk
    - Increase speed / ease of developing new systems
    - Enhance relationships with clients / customers
    - Uncover new ideas and insights
    - Encourage innovation and growth
    - Improve efficiency and productivity
    - Improve existing products and services
    - Shift workers from lower- to higher-value tasks
    - Increase revenue
    - Reduce costs

- **ROI findings for advanced initiatives**
  - “Almost all organizations report measurable ROI”
  - “one-fifth (20%) report ROI in excess of 30%.”
  - “nearly three-quarters (74%) say their most advanced initiative is meeting or exceeding their ROI expectations”
    - “43% meeting”
    - “31% exceeding”
  - “two-thirds (67%) say their most advanced initiative is at least moderately integrated into their broader work processes”
  - ROI distribution to date for most advanced initiative:
    - 51% or more = **6%**
    - 31% to 50% = **14%**
    - 11% to 30% = **23%**
    - 6% to 10% = **41%**
    - Less than 5% = **9%**
    - Not measuring ROI to date = **5%**
  - ROI expectations:
    - Significantly above = **7%**
    - Somewhat above = **24%**
    - Meeting = **19%**
    - Somewhat below = **43%**
    - Significantly below = **5%**
  - Integration level:
    - Completely integrated = **4%**
    - Large extent = **20%**
    - Moderate extent = **25%**
    - Small extent = **43%**
    - Not at all, but intend to = **7%**
    - No intention to integrate = **2%**
  - Cybersecurity-specific ROI and integration:
    - “44% of cybersecurity initiatives delivering an ROI somewhat or significantly above expectations”
    - “only 17% that are delivering an ROI somewhat or significantly below expectations”
    - “a 27-point gap”
    - “36% of respondents said their cybersecurity initiative is integrated into work processes to a large extent—a higher level of integration than any other kind of advanced GenAI initiative.”
  - ROI by function gaps:
    - R&D = **-5**
    - Operations = **0**
    - Sales = **-8**
    - Finance = **-8**
    - Product dev = **0**
    - Marketing = **+2**
    - Strategy = **+10**
    - Customer service = **+8**
    - Supply chain = **+7**
    - IT = **+15**
    - Cybersecurity = **+27**
  - “With advanced GenAI implementations in functions such as sales, finance and R&D, more respondents reported ROI below expectations than reported ROI above expectations.”
  - “Some initiatives are already exceeding expectations, but others are currently falling short.”

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors**
  - “agentic AI currently appears to be capturing the most interest and attention.”
  - Interest in future GenAI developments:
    - GenAI for automation (agentic AI) = **52%**
    - Multiagent systems = **45%**
    - Multimodal capabilities = **44%**
    - New training techniques = **35%**
    - Smaller, less resource-intensive models = **35%**
    - Alternative / improved architectures = **30%**
    - Synthetic data for training / tuning = **28%**
    - Large action models = **21%**
    - Advanced hardware specifically for GenAI applications = **20%**
  - “26% of our survey respondents said their organizations were already exploring autonomous agent development to a large or very large extent.”
  - Agentic AI success factors / operational guidance explicitly stated:
    - “developing a strategic road map”
    - “assessing which tasks and workflows are well-suited for agentic AI”
    - “Identify specific goals and desired value.”
    - “Map out the risks associated with autonomous agents and create mitigation plans.”
    - “Start with low-risk use cases that use noncritical data—with human oversight as a backup.”
    - “These early steps can help test and build the data management, cybersecurity and governance capabilities necessary for safe agentic AI applications.”
    - “Once your organization is comfortable, it can then progress to applications that use more proprietary data, have access to more tools, and operate more autonomously.”
  - Agentic AI caution:
    - “agentic AI is not a silver bullet”
    - “all the broad challenges currently facing GenAI still apply”
  - Named agentic AI use case example:
    - “specialized AI agents tailored to specific functions, like sales research, to manage the overwhelming volume of data”
    - “These agents will streamline processes, helping sales teams gather critical information quickly—without the need for extensive manual research.”
    - “Multiagent workflows are a future possibility; however, we anticipate starting with single-agent solutions that can mature and scale efficiently, focusing on ROI as they evolve into production.”

- **Failure modes / bottlenecks / negative outcomes**
  - “Most organizations are moving at the speed of organizations, not at the speed of technology.”
  - “creating value with GenAI—and deploying it at scale—is hard work.”
  - “there is no magic wand when it comes to GenAI adoption, deployment, integration and value creation.”
  - “accessing the right data proved to be the biggest bottleneck.”

title: State of Generative AI Q4 – Press Release
content:
- **Page relevance:** Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases because it contains survey findings on GenAI adoption, scaling, ROI, governance, risk barriers, and agentic AI.
- **Survey basis / scope**
  - “The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise: Generating a new future,” is based on a survey of **2,773 director- to C-suite-level respondents across 14 countries**.
  - The survey was conducted **between July and September 2024**.
  - Respondents were “experienced with AI and are piloting or implementing GenAI in their organizations.”
  - The wave connected with **2,773 AI-savvy business and technology leaders** across **14 countries and six industries: consumer; energy, resources and industrials; financial services; life sciences and health care; technology, media and telecom; and government and public services**.

- **Named functions / use cases / industry examples**
  - The report features case studies covering:
    - “how GenAI is boosting software security in banking”
    - “how it’s accelerating sales success in the technology industry”
    - “how it’s powering social media content creation in the consumer industry”
  - “GenAI usage in IT appears to be furthest along, with **28%** saying their most advanced initiative is in that function.”
  - “Cybersecurity implementations have also emerged as a standout, with **44%** saying ROI has surpassed their expectations, more than any other function.”

- **Quantitative estimates and adoption / scaling findings**
  - “more than **two-thirds** of respondents reporting that **30% or fewer** of their experiments will be fully scaled in the next three to six months.”
  - “nearly **three-quarters** of respondents reported that their most advanced GenAI initiative is meeting or exceeding ROI expectations.”
  - “a vast majority of respondents (**78%**) expect to increase their overall AI spending in the next fiscal year”
  - “Concerns around regulatory compliance has emerged as the top barrier holding organizations back from developing and deploying GenAI tools and applications – increasing **10 percentage points** from the Wave 1 survey (**28%**) to Wave 4 (**38%**).”
  - “**69%** of respondents say fully implementing a governance strategy will take over a year to resolve”
  - “Almost all organizations report measurable ROI, and almost a quarter (**20%**) report **31% or more**.”
  - “**26%** of surveyed organizations already exploring autonomous agent development to a large extent and **42%** to some extent.”
  - Key takeaways also state:
    - “**26%** of organizations currently exploring autonomous agent development to a large extent”
    - “more than two-thirds of respondents reporting that **30% or fewer** of their experiments will be fully scaled in the next three to six months”
    - “nearly three-quarters of respondents reported that their most advanced GenAI initiative is meeting or exceeding ROI expectations”

- **ROI findings**
  - “nearly three-quarters of respondents reported that their most advanced GenAI initiative is meeting or exceeding ROI expectations.”
  - “Almost all organizations report measurable ROI”
  - “almost a quarter (**20%**) report **31% or more**.”
  - “Cybersecurity implementations have also emerged as a standout, with **44%** saying ROI has surpassed their expectations, more than any other function.”
  - “Cybersecurity and IT functions are leading the way in terms of ROI and successful scaling.”

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors**
  - “Agentic AI is seen as a key enabler of sustainable value”
  - “26% of organizations currently exploring autonomous agent development to a large extent”
  - “42% to some extent”
  - “As software systems that can meet objectives with minimal intervention, agents could help accelerate the creation of long-lasting business value”
  - “future-thinking organizations are as bullish as ever in building bridges to ROI”
  - “the need for nuance — and patience — as we embrace this next wave of GenAI”
  - “with a focus on governance, collaboration and continued iteration as key accelerators in the race for sustainable value.”
  - “organizations are making strides with centralized governance, phased adoption, collaborative partnerships and continuous iteration.”
  - “Focus is essential, prioritizing demonstrated use cases with measurable return on investment.”
  - “To act decisively in the face of uncertainty, organizations should focus on market sensing and scenario planning”

- **Governance / risk obligations / barriers**

  - “Concerns around regulatory compliance has emerged as the top barrier holding organizations back from developing and deploying GenAI tools and applications”
  - “69% of respondents say fully implementing a governance strategy will take over a year to resolve”
  - “the need for disciplined action has grown”

  - “with a focus on governance, collaboration and continued iteration as key accelerators”

title: AI RMF Core - AIRC
content:
- Page relevance:
  - Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases because it defines AI risk management functions, lifecycle actions, governance obligations, measurement/monitoring, deployment go/no-go decision support, and failure/response handling relevant to enterprise AI pipelines.
  - No direct adoption statistics, ROI findings, market adoption rates, or named enterprise product use cases are stated on the page.

- Quantitative estimates:
  - None stated.
  - No percentages, counts, cost/ROI figures, benchmarks, or adoption numbers are provided.

- Named functions / use cases:
  - Four AI RMF Core functions are named:
    - govern
    - map
    - measure
    - manage
  - The AI RMF Core “provides outcomes and actions that enable dialogue, understanding, and activities to manage AI risks and responsibly develop trustworthy AI systems.”
  - The AI RMF Playbook is named as “an online companion resource” with “suggested tactical actions.”
  - The Playbook is “voluntary.”
  - The playbook is part of the “NIST Trustworthy and Responsible AI Resource Center.”
  - The “map” function supports:
    - “an initial decision about appropriateness or the need for an AI solution”
    - “an initial go/no-go decision about whether to design, develop, or deploy an AI system”
    - “model management”
  - The “measure” function uses “quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-method tools, techniques, and methodologies” to:
    - analyze
    - assess
    - benchmark
    - monitor AI risk and related impacts
  - The “manage” function entails:
    - allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks
    - risk treatment plans to respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events

- Governance / risk obligations:
  - “Risk management should be continuous, timely, and performed throughout the AI system lifecycle dimensions.”
  - AI RMF Core functions should be carried out with “diverse and multidisciplinary perspectives,” potentially including “AI actors outside the organization.”
  - Governance is “a cross-cutting function” and “infused throughout AI risk management.”
  - Aspects of govern “especially those related to compliance or evaluation, should be integrated into each of the other functions.”
  - “Attention to governance is a continual and intrinsic requirement for effective AI risk management over an AI system’s lifespan and the organization’s hierarchy.”
  - Strong governance:
    - can “drive and enhance internal practices and norms”
    - can “facilitate organizational risk culture”
    - governing authorities can determine policies directing “mission, goals, values, culture, and risk tolerance”
    - senior leadership “sets the tone for risk management”
    - management aligns technical aspects of AI risk management to policies and operations
    - documentation can “enhance transparency, improve human review processes, and bolster accountability”
  - Organizations should continue to execute govern as “knowledge, cultures, and needs or expectations from AI actors evolve over time.”
  - After map, users should have sufficient contextual knowledge to inform a go/no-go decision; if proceeding, organizations should utilize measure and manage along with govern policies and procedures.
  - After measure, “objective, repeatable, or scalable test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) processes” should be in place, followed, and documented.
  - Metrics and measurement methodologies should “adhere to scientific, legal, and ethical norms” and be carried out “in an open and transparent process.”
  - Manage requires “plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring and improvement.”
  - Manage includes “mechanisms for continual improvement.”
  - Manage includes “post-deployment AI system monitoring plans.”
  - Manage includes “appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.”

- Workflow / agentic AI success factors:
  - A diverse team contributes to “more open sharing of ideas and assumptions” and can “surface problems and identify existing and emergent risks.”
  - The playbook helps organizations “navigate the AI RMF and achieve its outcomes through suggested tactical actions” that they can apply within their own contexts.
  - Playbook users can “create tailored guidance selected from suggested material for their own use” and “contribute their suggestions for sharing with the broader community.”
  - Implementation of map is enhanced by:
    - “incorporating perspectives from a diverse internal team”
    - engagement with “collaborators, end users, potentially impacted communities, and others”
  - Gathering broad perspectives can help organizations:
    - “improve their capacity for understanding contexts”
    - “check their assumptions about context of use”
    - “enable recognition of when systems are not functional within or out of their intended context”
    - “identify positive and beneficial uses of their existing AI systems”
    - “improve understanding of limitations in AI and ML processes”
    - “identify constraints in real-world applications that may lead to negative impacts”
    - “identify known and foreseeable negative impacts related to intended use of AI systems”
    - “anticipate risks of the use of AI systems beyond intended use”
  - Map should support “context-specific laws, norms and expectations,” “prospective settings,” and “system requirements.”
  - Measure should include:
    - “rigorous software testing”
    - “performance assessment methodologies”
    - “measures of uncertainty”
    - “comparisons to performance benchmarks”
    - “formalized reporting and documentation of results”
    - “independent review”
  - Manage should include:
    - “resources required to manage AI risks”
    - “viable non-AI alternative systems, approaches, or methods”
    - “mechanisms … to sustain the value of deployed AI systems”
    - “procedures … to respond to and recover from a previously unknown risk”
    - responsibilities to “supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use”
  - Post-deployment monitoring should capture and evaluate:
    - input from users
    - input from other relevant AI actors
    - appeal and override
    - decommissioning
    - incident response
    - recovery
    - change management

- Failure modes / risk conditions:
  - “The interdependencies between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably anticipate impacts of AI systems.”
  - “Early decisions in identifying purposes and objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities.”
  - “The dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI system decisions.”
  - “The best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.”
  - “This complexity and varying levels of visibility can introduce uncertainty into risk management practices.”
  - “Without contextual knowledge, and awareness of risks within the identified contexts, risk management is difficult to perform.”
  - Measure recognizes that tradeoffs among trustworthy characteristics may arise.
  - Options in response to such tradeoffs may include:
    - recalibration
    - impact mitigation
    - removal of the system from design
    - removal of the system from development
    - removal of the system from production
    - removal of the system from use
    - compensating controls
    - detective controls
    - deterrent controls
    - directive controls
    - recovery controls
  - Measure 2.6 states AI systems should be safe, residual negative risk should not exceed risk tolerance, and they “can fail safely, particularly if made to operate beyond its knowledge limits.”
  - Manage 1.4 defines “negative residual risks” as “the sum of all unmitigated risks.”
  - Manage 2.3 addresses “a previously unknown risk.”
  - Manage 2.4 addresses AI systems that demonstrate “performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use.”
  - Govern 1.7 requires safe decommissioning and phasing out “in a manner that does not increase risks or decrease the organization’s trustworthiness.”
  - Govern 6.2 requires contingency processes for “failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems deemed to be high-risk.”
  - Measure 3.2 addresses settings where AI risks are difficult to assess using currently available measurement techniques or where metrics are not yet available.
  - Measure 3.3 includes user and community “report problems and appeal system outcomes.”
  - Manage 4.3 requires incidents and errors to be communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities.

- Governance / compliance / supply chain obligations:
  - Govern 1.1: “Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented.”
  - Govern 1.2: “The characteristics of trustworthy AI are integrated into organizational policies, processes, procedures, and practices.”
  - Govern 1.3: “Processes, procedures, and practices are in place to determine the needed level of risk management activities based on the organization’s risk tolerance.”
  - Govern 1.4: “The risk management process and its outcomes are established through transparent policies, procedures, and other controls based on organizational risk priorities.”
  - Govern 1.5: “Ongoing monitoring and periodic review” are planned and organizational roles and responsibilities clearly defined, including review frequency.
  - Govern 1.6: “Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities.”
  - Govern 1.7: “Processes and procedures are in place for decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely.”
  - Govern 2.1: Roles/responsibilities and lines of communication are documented and clear.
  - Govern 2.2: Personnel and partners receive AI risk management training.
  - Govern 2.3: Executive leadership takes responsibility for AI development and deployment risk decisions.
  - Govern 3.1: Decision-making is informed by a diverse team.
  - Govern 3.2: Policies and procedures define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight.
  - Govern 4.1: Policies and practices foster “critical thinking and safety-first mindset.”
  - Govern 4.2: Teams document risks and potential impacts and communicate about the impacts more broadly.
  - Govern 4.3: Organizational practices enable AI testing, identification of incidents, and information sharing.
  - Govern 5.1: Policies/practices collect, consider, prioritize, and integrate feedback from those external to the team.
  - Govern 5.2: Mechanisms enable regular incorporation of adjudicated feedback into system design and implementation.
  - Govern 6.1: Policies and procedures address AI risks associated with third-party entities, including “risks of infringement of a third-party’s intellectual property or other rights.”
  - Govern 6.2: Contingency processes handle failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems deemed high-risk.
  - Map 4.1 includes legal risks and third-party data/software risks, including infringement of IP or other rights.
  - Measure 2.10 examines and documents privacy risk.
  - Measure 2.11 evaluates fairness and bias.
  - Measure 2.12 assesses environmental impact and sustainability of AI model training and management activities.
  - Measure 2.7 evaluates security and resilience.
  - Measure 2.8 examines transparency and accountability risks.
  - Measure 2.9 requires model explanation, validation, documentation, and interpretation within context for responsible use and governance.
  - Manage 3.1: third-party risks and benefits are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented.
  - Manage 3.2: pre-trained models used for development are monitored as part of regular monitoring and maintenance.

- Adoption / ROI findings:
  - None stated on the page.

- Structured tables

| Area | Explicitly stated information |
|--|--|
| Quantitative estimates | None stated |
| Adoption findings | None stated |
| ROI findings | None stated |
| Named functions | govern, map, measure, manage |
| Companion resource | NIST AI RMF Playbook |
| Main lifecycle guidance | continuous, timely risk management throughout the AI system lifecycle |
| Decision point | initial go/no-go decision about whether to design, develop, or deploy an AI system |
| Monitoring | testing before deployment and regularly while in operation; post-deployment monitoring plans |
| Failure handling | incident response, recovery, change management, decommissioning, appeal/override, deactivate/supersede/disengage |

- Enumerations of listed subcategories with explicit wording

| Function | Categories and subcategories explicitly listed |
|--|--|
| Govern | Govern 1.1 through Govern 6.2 as shown in the page, including legal/regulatory requirements, trustworthy AI integration, risk tolerance, transparent policies, monitoring/review, inventory, decommissioning, accountability, training, leadership responsibility, diversity, human-AI configuration oversight, critical thinking/safety-first mindset, documentation/communication of risks and impacts, testing/incident sharing, external feedback, adjudicated feedback integration, third-party risks, and contingency processes |
| Map | Map 1.1 through Map 5.2 as shown in the page, including intended purposes, users, context-specific laws/norms, mission/goals, business value, risk tolerances, system requirements, task definitions, knowledge limits, TEVV considerations, benefits/costs, scope, operator proficiency, human oversight, third-party legal/technology risks, internal controls, impact characterization, and feedback integration |
| Measure | Measure 1.1 through Measure 4.3 as shown in the page, including selection of metrics, control assessment, independent assessors, TEVV documentation, human subject requirements, performance criteria, production monitoring, validity/reliability, safety, security/resilience, transparency/accountability, explanation/validation, privacy, fairness/bias, environmental impact, TEVV effectiveness, risk tracking, feedback/reporting, and consultation-informed measurements |
| Manage | Manage 1.1 through Manage 4.3 as shown in the page, including proceed/no-proceed determination, prioritization by impact/likelihood/resources, response planning, negative residual risk documentation, non-AI alternatives, sustaining value, responding to unknown risks, supersede/disengage/deactivate, third-party monitoring, pre-trained model monitoring, post-deployment monitoring, continual improvements, and incident/error communication |
