title: AI Act | Shaping Europe's digital future - European Union
content:
- **Page relevance for ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases**
  - Relevant for **governance, compliance, risk management, transparency, and implementation requirements** for AI systems and **GPAI models**.
  - **Not relevant for enterprise AI pipeline use-case performance ranking** in the sense of adoption metrics, ROI benchmarks, workflow throughput, or model comparison data.
  - The page contains **no quantitative adoption/ROI findings** for enterprise AI pipeline use cases.

- **Quantitative estimates / dates / timelines explicitly stated**
  - **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689**
  - **4 levels of risk** for AI systems
  - The AI Act prohibits **eight practices**
  - The prohibitions became effective in **February 2025**
  - Transparency rules will come into effect in **August 2026**
  - GPAI rules became effective in **August 2025**
  - The AI Act entered into force on **1 August 2024**
  - The AI Act will be fully applicable **2 years later on 2 August 2026**
  - Prohibited AI practices and AI literacy obligations entered into application from **2 February 2025**
  - Governance rules and obligations for GPAI models became applicable on **2 August 2025**
  - High-risk AI systems embedded into regulated products have an extended transition period until **2 August 2028**
  - The AI omnibus was **adopted on 19 November 2025**
  - A political agreement was reached on **7 May 2026**
  - Rules for systems used in certain high-risk areas will apply from **2 December 2027**
  - Rules for systems integrated into products such as lifts or toys will apply from **2 August 2028**
  - Support instruments for transparency rules “will be published in the **second quarter of 2026**”
  - The July 2026 action plan on Cybersecurity and AI is referenced
  - The call to increase EU evaluation capacity of AI models is “Expected to be operational by **2027**”

- **Named functions / use cases explicitly listed**
  - **AI-based manipulation and deception**
  - **AI-based exploitation of vulnerabilities**
  - **social scoring**
  - **Individual criminal offence risk assessment or prediction**
  - **untargeted scraping of the internet or CCTV material to create or expand facial recognition databases**
  - **emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions**
  - **biometric categorisation to deduce certain protected characteristics**
  - **real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement purposes in publicly accessible spaces**
  - **AI safety components in critical infrastructures (e.g. transport)**
  - **AI solutions used in education institutions**
  - **AI-based safety components of products (e.g. AI application in robot-assisted surgery)**
  - **AI tools for employment, management of workers and access to self-employment (e.g. CV-sorting software for recruitment)**
  - **Certain AI use-cases utilised to give access to essential private and public services (e.g. credit scoring denying citizens opportunity to obtain a loan)**
  - **AI systems used for remote biometric identification, emotion recognition and biometric categorisation (e.g. AI system to retroactively identify a shoplifter)**
  - **AI use-cases in law enforcement**
  - **AI use-cases in migration, asylum and border control management (e.g. automated examination of visa applications)**
  - **AI solutions used in the administration of justice and democratic processes (e.g. AI solutions to prepare court rulings)**
  - **chatbots**
  - **generative AI**
  - **deep fakes**
  - **text published with the purpose to inform the public on matters of public interest**
  - **General-purpose AI (GPAI) models**
  - **AI-generated content**
  - **AI systems built on general-purpose AI models**
  - **AI systems integrated into products such as lifts or toys**
  - **AI models for cybersecurity purposes**
  - **advanced AI systems for cybersecurity purposes**
  - **secure testing platform** for organisations in critical sectors
  - **AI solutions** for **energy, transport, health, finance and public administration**
  - **AI Act Whistleblower Tool**

- **Adoption / ROI / implementation findings explicitly stated**
  - “The vast majority of AI systems currently used in the EU fall into” **minimal or no risk**
  - “General-purpose AI (GPAI) models can perform a wide range of tasks and are becoming the basis for many AI systems in the EU.”
  - “Some of these models could carry systemic risks if they are very capable or widely used.”
  - The AI Act and related measures are intended to “strengthen uptake, investment and innovation in AI across the EU.”
  - The AI Act rules for GPAI provide “a clear and actionable framework” and are designed to work “hand-in-hand.”
  - These tools are said to reduce “administrative burden” and foster innovation while safeguarding fundamental rights and public trust.
  - The Digital Package on Simplification aims to make rules “clear, simple, and innovation-friendly.”
  - The extended timelines “ensure the rules apply when companies have the right support tools to facilitate implementation, such as standards.”
  - “More innovators will gain access to regulatory sandboxes, including an EU-level sandbox, to test their AI solutions in real-world conditions.”
  - The AI Act’s implementation support includes the AI Pact, AI Act Service Desk, guidelines, codes of practice, and the AI Office.

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors explicitly stated**
  - For high-risk AI systems:
    - **adequate risk assessment and mitigation systems**
    - **high-quality of the datasets feeding the system to minimise risks of discriminatory outcomes**
    - **logging of activity to ensure traceability of results**
    - **detailed documentation providing all information necessary on the system and its purpose for authorities to assess its compliance**
    - **clear and adequate information to the deployer**
    - **appropriate human oversight measures**
    - **high level of robustness, cybersecurity and accuracy**
  - For transparency obligations:
    - Humans should be made aware that they are interacting with a machine when using AI systems such as **chatbots**
    - Providers of generative AI have to ensure that **AI-generated content is identifiable**
    - Certain AI-generated content should be **clearly and visibly labelled**, namely **deep fakes** and **text published with the purpose to inform the public on matters of public interest**
  - Supporting compliance for GPAI models:
    - The **GPAI Code of Practice** is a voluntary compliance tool offering practical guidance for **transparency, copyright, and safety & security**
    - The **Template for the public summary of training content of GPAI models** requires providers to give an overview of the data used to train their models
    - The template includes the **sources from which the data was obtained (comprising large datasets and top domain names)**
    - It also requests information about **data processing aspects** to enable parties with legitimate interests to exercise their rights under EU law

- **Governance / risk obligations explicitly stated**
  - The AI Act sets out a **risk-based rules** framework for AI developers and deployers regarding specific uses of AI.
  - **All AI systems considered a clear threat to the safety, livelihoods and rights of people are banned.**
  - **High-risk AI systems are subject to strict obligations before they can be put on the market.**
  - **Once an AI system is on the market, authorities are in charge of market surveillance, deployers ensure human oversight and monitoring, and providers have a post-market monitoring system in place.**
  - **Providers and deployers will also report serious incidents and malfunctioning.**
  - For GPAI models, the AI Act includes **transparency and copyright-related rules**.
  - For models that may carry systemic risks, providers should **assess and mitigate these risks**.
  - The European AI Office and authorities of the Member States are responsible for **implementing, supervising and enforcing the AI Act**.
  - The **AI Board, the Scientific Panel and the Advisory Forum** steer and advise the AI Act’s governance.
  - The Commission and **ENISA** will create:
    - a **blueprint to secure access to advanced AI systems for cybersecurity purposes**
    - a **secure testing platform** to help organisations in critical sectors safely test and deploy AI solutions

- **Failure modes / risks explicitly stated**
  - It is often not possible to find out **why an AI system has made a decision or prediction and taken a particular action**.
  - This can make it difficult to assess whether someone has been **unfairly disadvantaged**, such as in:
    - **a hiring decision**
    - **an application for a public benefit scheme**
  - Certain AI systems create **risks** that must be addressed to avoid **undesirable outcomes**.
  - High-risk AI systems can pose serious risks to **health, safety or fundamental rights**.
  - Risks include **discriminatory outcomes** from poor dataset quality.
  - GPAI models could carry **systemic risks** if they are very capable or widely used.
  - The page references **cybersecurity and resilience challenges posed by the most advanced AI models**.
  - The page references the need to address **malfunctioning** and **serious incidents**.

- **Exact prohibitions / list**
  - The **AI Act prohibits eight practices**, namely:
    1. harmful AI-based manipulation and deception
    2. harmful AI-based exploitation of vulnerabilities
    3. social scoring
    4. Individual criminal offence risk assessment or prediction
    5. untargeted scraping of the internet or CCTV material to create or expand facial recognition databases
    6. emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions
    7. biometric categorisation to deduce certain protected characteristics
    8. real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement purposes in publicly accessible spaces

- **High-risk AI systems include**
  - AI safety components in critical infrastructures (e.g. transport), the failure of which could put the life and health of citizens at risk
  - AI solutions used in education institutions, that may determine the access to education and course of someone’s professional life (e.g. scoring of exams)
  - AI-based safety components of products (e.g. AI application in robot-assisted surgery)
  - AI tools for employment, management of workers and access to self-employment (e.g. CV-sorting software for recruitment)
  - Certain AI use-cases utilised to give access to essential private and public services (e.g. credit scoring denying citizens opportunity to obtain a loan)
  - AI systems used for remote biometric identification, emotion recognition and biometric categorisation (e.g. AI system to retroactively identify a shoplifter)
  - AI use-cases in law enforcement that may interfere with people’s fundamental rights (e.g. evaluation of the reliability of evidence)
  - AI use-cases in migration, asylum and border control management (e.g. automated examination of visa applications)
  - AI solutions used in the administration of justice and democratic processes (e.g. AI solutions to prepare court rulings)

- **High-risk AI systems strict obligations**
  - adequate risk assessment and mitigation systems
  - high-quality of the datasets feeding the system to minimise risks of discriminatory outcomes
  - logging of activity to ensure traceability of results
  - detailed documentation providing all information necessary on the system and its purpose for authorities to assess its compliance
  - clear and adequate information to the deployer
  - appropriate human oversight measures
  - high level of robustness, cybersecurity and accuracy

- **General-purpose AI model obligations / support instruments**
  - The AI Act rules on GPAI became effective in **August 2025**.
  - In **July 2025**, the Commission published **3 key instruments**:
    - **The Guidelines on the scope of the obligations for providers of GPAI models**
    - **The GPAI Code of Practice**
    - **The Template for the public summary of training content of GPAI models**
  - The guidelines clarify the scope of the GPAI obligations under the AI Act.
  - The GPAI Code of Practice is a **voluntary compliance tool**.
  - It offers practical guidance related to **transparency, copyright, and safety & security**.
  - The template requires providers to give an overview of the data used to train their models.
  - The template includes the sources from which the data was obtained, **comprising large datasets and top domain names**.
  - The template also requests information about data processing aspects to enable parties with legitimate interests to exercise their rights under EU law.

- **Transparency obligations**
  - The AI Act introduces specific disclosure obligations to ensure that humans are informed when necessary to preserve trust.
  - When using AI systems such as chatbots, humans should be made aware that they are interacting with a machine.
  - Providers of generative AI have to ensure that AI-generated content is identifiable.
  - Deep fakes and text published with the purpose to inform the public on matters of public interest should be clearly and visibly labelled.

- **Governance bodies / implementation**
  - The **European AI Office**
  - **authorities of the Member States**
  - The **AI Board**
  - The **Scientific Panel**
  - The **Advisory Forum**
  - The **AI Office** is also referenced in relation to selected code of practice and oversight of AI systems built on GPAI models.

title: Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 - www-api.ibm.com
content:
- **Relevance to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases**
  - The page is relevant because it includes explicit findings on:
    - AI-related breaches
    - AI governance
    - AI-driven attacks
    - Security AI and automation
    - Shadow AI
    - Operational disruption and recovery
    - Governance/risk obligations and failure modes
  - It does **not** provide a ranked list of “enterprise AI pipeline use cases” by business value or adoption. It provides evidence relevant to prioritizing AI-related security, governance, and operational risk use cases.

- **Quantitative estimates and named AI-related functions/use cases**
  - **13%** of organizations reported breaches that involved their **AI models or applications**.
  - **97%** of organizations that reported an AI-related breach **lacked proper AI access controls**.
  - The most common AI security incident cause was **supply chain compromise (30%)**, including **compromised apps, APIs and plug-ins**.
  - Other AI incident types:
    - **Model inversion: 24%**
    - **Model evasion: 21%**
    - **Prompt injection: 17%**
    - **Data poisoning: 15%**
  - Impacts of AI security incidents:
    - **Operational disruptions: 31%**
    - **Unauthorized access to sensitive data: 31%**
    - **Loss of data integrity: 29%**
    - **Financial loss: 23%**
    - **Reputational damage: 17%**
  - Source/hosting of AI in incidents:
    - **Third-party vendor, delivered as SaaS: 29%**
    - **Third-party vendor, deployed on premises: 19%**
    - **Open source: 26%**
    - **Trained in-house: 26%**
  - **Shadow AI**
    - **20%** of breaches involved security incidents with **shadow AI**.
    - **11%** of breached organizations were **unsure** if they experienced a shadow AI incident.
    - Breaches with high levels of shadow AI added **USD 670,000** to the average breach price tag.
    - Shadow AI incidents caused:
      - **More personal identifiable information (65%)** compromised
      - **Intellectual property (40%)** compromised
    - Shadow AI incidents contributed **USD 200,000** to the global average breach cost.
    - Average time of a breach that included unsanctioned or shadow AI:
      - **MTTI 62**
      - **MTTC 185**
      - **Total 247 days**
      - Compared with global cost of a data breach:
        - **MTTI 60**
        - **MTTC 181**
        - **Total 241 days**
  - **Security AI and automation**
    - **32%** used security AI and automation **extensively**
    - **40%** used them in a **limited way**
    - **28%** used them **not at all**
    - Extensive use lowered average breach costs to **USD 3.62 million** versus **USD 5.52 million** for no use.
    - Extensive use shortened breach times by **80 days** compared to no use.
    - AI and automation use across workflows:
      - **Prevention: 30% limited, 27% none, 43% extensive**
      - **Detection: 29% limited, 27% none, 44% extensive**
      - **Investigation: 26% limited, 28% none, 46% extensive**
      - **Response: 27% limited, 28% none, 45% extensive**
    - **77%** were either adopting AI at par with or more advanced than their wider organization:
      - **43% roughly on par**
      - **34% more advanced**
      - **23% less adoption**
  - **AI-driven attacks**
    - **16%** of breaches involved attackers using AI.
    - AI-driven attack types:
      - **AI-generated phishing or other communication: 37%**
      - **AI deepfake attacks: 35%**
    - IBM previously found gen AI reduced the time needed to craft a convincing phishing email from **16 hours down to only five minutes**.
  - **Recovery and business disruption**
    - **86%** of organizations experienced operational disruption due to a data breach.
    - **35%** said they had **fully recovered** from the data breach.
    - **65%** said they were **still recovering**.
    - Among fully recovered organizations:
      - **76%** said recovery took longer than **100 days**
      - **26%** said recovery took more than **150 days**
      - **2%** said recovery was possible within as little as **50 days**

- **Adoption / ROI findings**
  - Security teams using AI and automation extensively:
    - shortened breach times by **80 days**
    - lowered average breach costs by **USD 1.9 million**
  - Security teams using AI and machine-learning insights had average breach costs of **USD 3.85 million** versus **USD 4.90 million** for low/no use.
  - DevSecOps approach:
    - **USD 3.89 million** with high use versus **USD 5.02 million** with low/no use.
  - Security analytics or SIEM:
    - **USD 3.91 million** with high use versus **USD 4.83 million** with low/no use.
  - Post-breach investment:
    - **49%** said they would increase security investments following a breach.
    - **45%** of post-breach organizations said they would choose **AI-driven solutions**.
  - Among organizations planning to invest in AI-driven solutions post-breach, categories included:
    - **Threat detection and response: 36%**
    - **IR planning and testing: 35%**
    - **Data security and protection tools: 31%**
    - **Managed security services: 29%**
    - **IAM: 28%**
    - **Offensive security testing: 28%**

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors**
  - **Protect identity and access**
    - “Fortifying identity security with the help of AI and automation can improve IAM without overburdening chronically understaffed security teams.”
    - Organizations should maintain visibility into all **non-human identity (NHI)** activity.
    - Organizations must distinguish between NHIs using **managed (vaulted) credentials** and those using **unmanaged credentials**.
    - Credential lifecycle management and governance should include:
      - **provisioning**
      - **rotation**
      - **auditing**
      - **protection**
      - **decommissioning**
    - Prevent attackers from obtaining credentials by ensuring all human users adopt **modern, phishing-resistant authentication methods, such as passkeys**.
  - **Secure AI data**
    - Needed controls:
      - **data discovery and classification**
      - **access control**
      - **encryption**
      - **key management**
      - **data and AI security services**
  - **Connect security for AI and governance for AI**
    - The report says these are **complementary disciplines**.
    - Investments in **integrated security and governance software and processes** can help organizations:
      - gain visibility into all AI deployments
      - identify and mitigate vulnerabilities
      - protect prompts and data generated from unintended use
      - use observability tools to improve compliance and detect anomalies
  - **Use AI security tools and automation to move faster**
    - Security tools and managed security services powered by AI and automation can:
      - reduce the volume of alerts
      - identify at-risk data
      - spot security gaps and threats earlier
      - detect in-progress breaches
      - enable faster, more precise attack responses
  - **Improve resilience**
    - Resilience planning should include:
      - regularly testing IR plans
      - restoration of backups
      - clear roles and responsibilities during crisis response
      - limiting high-level access
      - in-person or virtual training
      - cyber range crisis simulation exercises

- **Governance / risk obligations**
  - **63%** of breached organizations either don’t have an **AI governance policy** or are still developing one.
  - **37%** had AI governance policies in place.
  - Among organizations with AI governance policies:
    - **45%** had **strict approval processes for AI deployments**
    - **39%** used **AI governance technology**
    - **39%** used **AI governance frameworks**
    - **36%** provided **employee training on AI risks**
    - **34%** performed **regular audits for unsanctioned AI**
    - **22%** used **adversarial testing**
  - **87%** of organizations said they have **no governance policies or processes to mitigate AI risk**.
  - **41%** of organizations said they didn’t have such policies in place, and **22%** are still developing them.
  - The report explicitly states oversight of AI and the ability to identify shadow AI is **essential** for ensuring the **ethical, legal and responsible development and use of AI among employees**.
  - The report says **CISOs, CROs and CCOs** and their teams should collaborate regularly.
  - It also states organizations should invest in integrated security and governance software and processes to **automatically discover and govern shadow AI**.
  - For AI model evasion risk assessment:
    - **50%** use internal risk assessment teams
    - **38%** use automated risk assessment tools
    - **34%** rely on third-party security audits
  - Breach-related compliance obligations:
    - Recovery definition includes organizations having **met compliance obligations, such as paying fines**.
  - Regulatory fine data:
    - **32%** of data breaches resulted in fines.
    - **48%** of those fines were above **USD 100,000**.

- **Failure modes / risk patterns**
  - Organizations are “skipping over security and governance for AI in favor of do-it-now AI adoption.”
  - Ungoverned AI systems are “more likely to be breached—and more costly when they are.”
  - The most common AI incident cause was **supply chain compromise**, including **compromised apps, APIs or plug-ins**.
  - AI incidents led to:
    - broad data compromise (**60%** of AI-related breaches, from the key findings section)
    - operational disruption (**31%**)
  - Shadow AI can go undetected and be exploited when employees use it.
  - Shadow AI incidents were associated with:
    - greater breach cost
    - more PII compromise
    - more IP compromise
    - longer detection and containment times
  - Security system complexity and supply chain breaches are highlighted as cost amplifiers.
  - Malicious or criminal attacks continue to dominate root causes at **51%**.
  - Human error (**26%**) and IT failure (**23%**) remain significant root causes.
  - Malicious insider attacks were the costliest initial attack vector at **USD 4.92 million**.
  - Third-party vendor and supply chain compromise was **USD 4.91 million** and took **267 days** to resolve.
  - Phishing was the most common initial attack vector at **16%**, averaging **USD 4.80 million**.
  - Compromised credentials took **246 days** to resolve.
  - Data stored across multiple environments was the most time-consuming to resolve at **276 days**.
  - Healthcare breaches took **279 days** to identify and contain.
  - Breaches with a lifecycle over **200 days** cost **USD 5.01 million** versus **USD 3.87 million** for under **200 days**.

- **Other explicitly stated details relevant to prioritization**
  - Global average cost of a data breach: **USD 4.44 million**
  - United States average: **USD 10.22 million**
  - Security teams and tools detected **50%** of breaches, up from **42%** in 2024.
  - Breaches identified by internal security teams cost **USD 4.18 million** versus **USD 5.08 million** when disclosed by the attacker.
  - Internal security teams identified breaches in **172 days** and contained them in **240 days**.
  - In-house security teams and tools have improved breach detection performance over the past two years.
  - Less than half of organizations said they would pass breach costs on to customers (**45%** in 2025 vs **63%** in 2024).
  - **30%** said costs would be increased by **15% and above** among those passing costs on to customers.
  - The report states that security AI and automation is a consistent cost-lowering factor year over year.

- **Absence of requested item if looking for an explicit ranked “enterprise AI pipeline use cases” list**
  - No explicit ranking of enterprise AI pipeline use cases is provided.
  - No named “AI pipeline use cases” such as data ingestion, model training, inference, orchestration, retrieval, or agentic workflow steps are listed as enterprise use cases on this page.

title: Better supply-chain planning with AI and machine learning | McKinsey.org
content:
- **Page relevance**
  - Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases: it describes **AI and machine learning** applied to **end-to-end supply chain planning**, including named functions, adoption levels, ROI estimates, workflow/operating model changes, governance/KPI implications, and failure/limitation modes.

- **High-level AI use case / pipeline framing**
  - “**AI and machine learning** hold the potential to dramatically improve supply chain performance for consumer packaged goods (CPG) companies.”
  - The page argues against “a collection of point solutions” because they “**don’t talk to each other or integrate data**.”
  - The better approach is to “**integrate the entire end-to-end supply chain** so that they can run the majority of processes and decisions through **real-time, autonomous planning**.”
  - “Forecast changes in demand can be automatically factored into all processes and decisions along the chain, back to inventory, production planning and scheduling, and raw-material procurement.”

- **Quantitative estimates / ROI / performance impact**
  - “The experiences of a few major CPG companies show that autonomous supply chain planning can lead to:
    - “**an increase in revenue of up to 4 percent**”
    - “**a reduction in inventory of up to 20 percent**”
    - “**a decrease in supply chain costs of up to 10 percent**”
  - The article also states:
    - “leading to an **increase in revenue of 3 to 4 percent**”
    - “Inventory levels can decrease by **10 to 20 percent**”
    - “resulting in a reduction in supply chain costs of **5 to 10 percent**”
  - In the example company:
    - “The system could generate forecasts that were **10 to 12 percent more accurate at the individual SKU level**.”
    - “Inventory for finished goods decreased by **6 to 8 percent**.”
    - “Order fill rates increased by **3 to 5 percent**.”
  - Time/process performance:
    - The company “typically required **more than five days** to create a demand plan”
    - and “**more than two days** to create a dispatch plan.”
    - “In **three months**, the team developed minimum viable product (MVP) solutions...”

- **Adoption / market state findings**
  - McKinsey interviewed senior leaders from large CPG manufacturers in Asia.
  - “In our sample, **approximately 80 percent of companies still follow traditional or collaborative sales and operations planning (S&OP) processes**, with limited real-time decision making or automation.”
  - “At the same time, a small number of leading CPG companies (**7 percent in our sample**) have started to adopt autonomous end-to-end planning...”

- **Named functions / use cases explicitly mentioned**
  - “**S&OP**”
  - “**demand planning**”
  - “**inventory planning**”
  - “**dispatch planning**”
  - “**exception-planning**”
  - “**sales and operations planning (S&OP) processes**”
  - “**dynamic production scheduling**”
  - “**inventory and replenishments**”
  - “**exceptions management for expedited orders or other outliers**”
  - “**the integration of suppliers**”
  - “**forecasting**”
  - “**demand sensing**”
  - “**production schedule and plan**”
  - “**raw-material procurement**”
  - “**control tower planners**”
  - “**demand-planning analysts**”
  - “**agile coaches**”
  - “**workflow management**”
  - “**transportation management solutions**”
  - “**machine and deep learning**”
  - “**intelligent sensors**”
  - “**production facilities**”
  - “**individual pieces of manufacturing equipment**”

- **Workflow / agentic-AI-like operating model success factors**
  - Autonomous planning is described as a “**continuous, closed-loop planning approach** built on a **fully automated technology platform**.”
  - It is “designed to optimize S&OP processes in real time.”
  - It requires “**less direct human oversight and decision making**.”
  - Foundational principles:
    - “**Reduce human involvement**” by relying on automation to handle most processes end to end, with manual interventions only for exceptions and special circumstances.
    - “**Rely on integrated advanced analytics**” throughout the supply chain, creating “an explicit link from demand forecasts and orders back through to the production schedule and plan.”
    - “**Evolve from structured planning processes**” to “a more fluid approach, based on cross-functional and continuous touchpoints that can proactively integrate real-time information.”
    - “**Hard-wire processes and KPIs directly into business units**,” rather than concentrating ownership/control in the operations function.
    - “**Build the organizational capacity to evolve over time**,” by piloting new uses cases, learning from experience, and developing data and analytics capabilities.
  - The example company:
    - “assembled an **agile, cross-functional team**”
    - focused initially on “**three major planning functions**”
    - used “advanced analytics, machine-learning algorithms, and related tools”
    - collaborated with “marketing and sales to test that prediction through demand sensing and agree on the best path forward.”
  - The article says planning should increasingly be limited to “**managing rare exceptions**,” with AI and ML handling “**the bulk of standard processes**.”
  - Success depends on:
    - “**Cross-functional coordination and project-management capabilities**”
    - “**A mindset of accountability**”
    - “**Familiarity with enterprise-level software applications**”
    - “**An ability to segment products and customers** and understand concepts such as the total cost to serve.”

- **Governance / risk / performance-management obligations**
  - Companies need to think beyond technology to include:
    - “**process redesign**”
    - “**talent**”
    - “**performance management**”
    - “and other aspects of operations.”
  - The organizational design “can have a critical impact on overall performance.”
  - To coordinate autonomous planning across business units/functions/sites, organizations can create formal roles:
    - “**demand-planning analysts**”
    - “**control tower planners**”
    - “**S&OP facilitators**”
    - “**agile coaches**”
  - “**KPIs will likely need to be defined for the entire supply chain organization**,” with everyone incentivized toward the right target behaviors.
  - Many companies “still set performance targets within individual functions or business units.”
  - Companies may need to “**redesign their performance-management systems** to be more integrated and cohesive.”
  - “Operations leaders do not need deep, highly technical knowledge” of the software, but need to understand:
    - “how they create transparency and improve performance”
    - “where they might have blind spots and require human intervention.”
  - Technology platform requirement:
    - “Autonomous planning rests on a technology platform with a **centralized data model**.”
  - On implementation approach:
    - “Some organizations believe they need to build a new tech stack... but that can slow down the process; we believe that companies can make faster progress by leveraging their existing stack.”
  - Sensing/prediction obligation:
    - Organizations need to pull data across the value chain from “**intelligent sensors**,” programmed to identify critical events, assess their impact, and adjust planning and control variables.
  - Risk modeling:
    - Software must be able to model disruptions, including:
      - “the total impact if a specific supplier goes down”
      - internal assets such as “production facilities”
      - “individual pieces of manufacturing equipment”
      - “the overall impact on service levels if a particular asset fails.”

- **Failure modes / limitations / risks explicitly stated**
  - Point solutions “**don’t talk to each other or integrate data**.”
  - This approach “still requires COOs and ops teams to be directly involved in decision making and oversight” to manage “junction points and interdependencies.”
  - Traditional planning depends on:
    - “unreliable sources of data”
    - “outdated IT systems”
    - “coordination limited across functions.”
  - Even data-based planners often optimize “**at the local level, rather than globally**,” with limited ability to address disruptions in real time.
  - Risks from traditional planning during rapid demand shifts:
    - “product shortages”
    - “increased costs from stock”
    - “inventory write-offs”
    - “related inefficiencies up and down the value chain.”
  - Execution can be “nearly impossible” if components of the system are not aligned.
  - Building a new tech stack “**can slow down the process**.”
  - Autonomous planning is “a journey” and “not a one-time transaction.”
  - Human blind spots:
    - software can have “blind spots and require human intervention.”
  - The evolution requires organizations to manage “rare exceptions” rather than assuming full elimination of human involvement.

- **Company example: specific details**
  - The company is described as:
    - “**one of the largest branded consumer food and beverage product companies in Asia**”
  - Historically used:
    - “traditional processes”
    - “an annual budget plan for forecasting”
    - “highly manual, rule-of-thumb decisions”
  - Initial focus areas:
    - demand planning
    - inventory planning
    - dispatch planning
  - Future expansion:
    - “exception-planning”
    - “sales and operations planning (S&OP) processes”
  - Ultimate goal:
    - “a single, comprehensive system that spans the entire supply chain.”

- **Page’s explicit strategic conclusion**
  - CPG manufacturers “can no longer rely on the supply chain planning processes of the past.”
  - They have “a clear opportunity to improve financial and operational performance by implementing autonomous planning across the entire end-to-end supply chain.”
description: Too many consumer-goods companies still rely on old-school, manual supply-chain planning—especially in Asia. For real-time decision making, automation is critical.

  - **Gas turbines**
  - **Pumps**

- **Barriers / failure modes for large-scale PdM**
  - **Data** is insufficient, inaccessible, or of low quality
  - **Technology** is inadequate, with too few sensors or poor IT infrastructure
  - **Prioritization** is difficult, as companies lack a clear view of which assets to include in their PdM programs
  - **Capabilities** are missing, especially the skilled data engineers and data scientists required to build advanced analytical models
  - **Change management** is weak, often because of user-unfriendly design
  - **Economic return** is low, due the high cost of developing models to cover diverse assets and numerous potential failure modes
  - “**high-value failure modes (such as in critical equipment) that occur at low frequency each year, making them harder for traditional methods or typical AI approaches to predict accurately**”
  - “**In early iterations, PdM models will often generate a significant number of false alarms**”
  - “**this behavior can undermine operating teams’ confidence in the model, creating the risk that they start to ignore warnings generated by the system**”
  - “**A model that generates numerous alarms may catch all the failures (high recall), but it is often incorrect and may not be trusted (low precision)**”
  - “**A predictive maintenance system is only valuable if it predicts the failure modes that cause value erosion**”
  - “**a long tail of root causes across machines and processes, which slowly changes as plants get older and processes, machines, software, and people’s behavior all evolve**”

- **Golden rules for successful implementation of predictive maintenance at scale**
  - “**Be judicious about which assets to include**”
  - “**Consider the right partners**”
  - “**Provide sufficient time to improve models**”
  - “**Put people first**”
  - “**Build predictive maintenance into the organization’s wider digital ecosystem**”

- **Golden Rule 1: Choose assets carefully**
  - “**Level 3.0 and 4.0 PdM implementations are now proven to work at scale**”
  - They require:
    - “**a certain level of Internet of Things (IoT) capability**”
    - “**a long data history**”
    - “**downtime of sufficient value to provide an attractive return on investment**”
  - “**Ultimately the decision on where to implement PdM requires an asset-by-asset validation of the potential benefits and data availability**”
  - Companies should prioritize assets that fulfill **three criteria**:
    - “**they are critical to operations, meaning failures can result in immediate loss of production**”
    - “**the assets have sufficient sensor coverage and data availability**”
      - validate “**the number and types of sensors installed**”
      - “**the availability and retrievability of historical data**”
      - “**the connectivity of online data**”
    - “**they are assets that have demonstrated sufficient past failure or anomaly behaviors**”
      - “**Assets with little failure history make it much harder to develop meaningful machine-learning models**”
  - Example prioritizations:
    - “**a renewable-power company prioritized the gear boxes of its wind turbines**”
    - “**an oil and gas company in Asia prioritized critical rotating equipment (such as the main air blower, compressors, gas turbines, and pumps)**”
    - “**several mining companies selected engines for the dump trucks and excavators as the critical equipment for their PdM implementations**”

- **Golden Rule 2: Tech partners matter**
  - “**The more sophisticated the approach for predictive maintenance, the more it requires a proven track record developed through heavy investments in knowledge, data, and development**”
  - “**PdM 4.0 is arguably more challenging to master than most digital and analytics use cases because of the complexity of initial modelling, model implementation, and ongoing model maintenance**”
  - “**the last mile: the change management involved in assuring that PdM tools are creating meaningful and tangible value is far from trivial**”
  - A right partner can help by:
    - “**providing training tailored to the personnel involved**”
    - “**engaging them throughout the deployment to ensure buy-in**”
    - “**integrating PdM actions into existing workflow systems**”
  - “**it rarely makes sense to develop these models in-house, especially from scratch**”
  - Partners can provide:
    - “**substantial intellectual property and data**”
    - “**significantly reducing both the time to impact and the investment required**”
  - “**Some of these vendors have emerged from within asset-intensive industries themselves, with technology offerings and IP based on years of experience developing and deploying PdM in large-scale real-world applications**”

- **Golden Rule 3: Allow time for continuous improvement**
  - Companies typically seek to improve **three aspects**:
    - **Precision**
      - “**the fraction of the alerts generated by the system that correspond to a real issue in the asset**”
      - “**PdM models will often generate a significant number of false alarms**”
      - “**the operating team needs to work with the PdM team as part of the deployment effort**”
      - “**Their consistent feedback will enable the modelers to improve precision and ensure that recommendations generated by the model are both accurate and actionable**”
    - **Recall**
      - “**the fraction of real-life issues with the asset that are predicted by the model**”
      - “**the metric that most directly indicates value capture**”
      - “**there is usually a trade-off with precision**”
      - “**With a multidisciplinary team and clear feedback from operations, models may be fine-tuned to achieve the best balance**”
    - **Breadth**
      - “**A predictive maintenance system is only valuable if it predicts the failure modes that cause value erosion**”
      - “**this typically means a long tail of root causes across machines and processes**”
      - “**many models are needed to capture substantial value in a plant (often exceeding triple digits)**”
      - “**continuous deployment of models addressing new root causes can be considered and pursued**”

- **Golden Rule 4: Put people first**
  - “**change management that puts the user at the center of the implementation is the single most critical success factor to ensure adoption at scale and achieve sustainable impact**”
  - “**Five elements together form a change-management program that supports the introduction of PdM**”
  - The five elements:
    1. “**an end-to-end process redesign that aims to provide clarity on roles and responsibilities post implementation, based on the collective design input from cross-functional teams**”
    2. “**sustained capability building**” to equip the organization with:
       - “**the immediate technical skills required for the digital solution**”
       - “**the long-term requirement for an internal pool of talent for data engineering, data science, and design thinking**”
    3. “**new KPIs and incentives are usually required**”
       - go “**beyond technical issues (such as model accuracy)**”
       - focus on “**broader leading and lagging indicators, such as unplanned-downtime reduction, adherence to internal maintenance-process timelines, and the adoption rate of the solution**”
       - “**Some companies even use digitized gamification to incentivize user adoption and usage**”
    4. “**top management also faces the task of transforming its collective mind-set to role model the new way of working and make their commitment to PdM visible to everyone**”
    5. “**a carefully crafted change story, regular omnichannel communication and campaigns, and bite-size microlearning nuggets can promote engagement across all levels of the organization**”

- **Golden Rule 5: Build PdM into the digital ecosystem**
  - “**Even the most sophisticated PdM system will create value only if it drives a response in the field: a set of actions that are clearly derived from the alarm the system generates**”
  - “**As a PdM system is scaled up, it becomes increasingly difficult to manage such actions consistently**”
  - “**creating tight links between PdM systems and other parts of the digital maintenance ecosystem**”
  - “**leading companies are integrating predictive maintenance technologies with new or existing digital work management (DWM) systems**”
  - Links work both directions:
    - “**Predictive maintenance alarms should trigger work orders in the DWM system**”
    - “**the results of those actions should then be fed back to the team managing the PdM system**”
  - Benefits:
    - “**allowing them to continuously improve its performance**”
    - “**The combination of PdM and DWM allows the performance and impact of the system to be measured effectively, creating accountability and justifying investments**”
    - “**Lessons learned from breakdowns or maintenance interventions can be stored in a knowledge base and shared among different teams, assets, and plants**”
    - “**The DWM system also aids the proactive planning of ongoing PdM developments**”
    - “**helping teams identify and prioritize opportunities to extend the assets and failure modes covered by the system**”
    - “**planners can adapt and optimize their preventative maintenance strategies to take full advantage of their growing predictive capabilities**”

- **Adoption / ROI findings**
  - “**few have been able to deploy PdM at scale across their operations**”
  - “**Level 3.0 and 4.0 PdM implementations are now proven to work at scale**”
  - “**This is the case in situations such as upstream oil and gas facilities, large refineries, petrochemical plants, power-generation facilities, paper mills, and mining operations**”
  - “**Predictive maintenance may not be the most economic maintenance strategy at this moment for certain other industries and assets**”
  - “**the value of reliability for large industrials typically lies in a wide range of equipment and failure modes**”
  - “**early adopters shows that success is possible**”
  - “**best-in-class industrial players have shown the way, capturing value from both increased uptime and reduced maintenance costs**”

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors explicitly stated**

  - “**bite-size microlearning nuggets**”

- **Governance / risk / organizational obligations explicitly stated**
  - “**asset-by-asset validation of the potential benefits and data availability**”
  - Validate “**the number and types of sensors installed**”

title: Setting the revenue cycle up for success in automation and AI
content:
- **Page relevance**
  - Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases in healthcare revenue cycle management.
  - Includes multiple named use cases, quantitative estimates, adoption/ROI findings, workflow considerations, governance/risk obligations, and failure modes.

- **Quantitative estimates and findings**
  - “effectively deploying automation and analytics alone could eliminate **$200 billion to $360 billion** of spending in US healthcare”
  - “Call centers have already improved their productivity by **15 to 30 percent** using gen AI.”
  - “**60 percent of denials may not be appealed at all**.”
  - “decrease accounts receivable days” is mentioned as a possible effect, but no number is provided.
  - “break even—net the cost of applied risk-mitigation strategies—may be a satisfactory outcome if holistic value is created elsewhere”

- **Named functions / use cases**
  - Revenue cycle management (RCM)
  - scheduling
  - coordinating care with insurers
  - documentation
  - claim or bill adjudication
  - voice recognition dictation software that “records, transcribes, and structures notes from physician–patient encounters” and “uses the information to complete administrative tasks in the background”
  - identify duplicate patient records
  - automate eligibility determination based on payer policies and contracts
  - coordinate prior authorizations from health insurance companies
  - propose solutions to address administrative gaps
  - improve clinical documentation accuracy
  - reduce clinicians’ time spent on recordkeeping
  - “pajama time” charting
  - accounts receivable with automated follow-ups
  - structure fact-based appeals to health insurers incorporating historical insurer performance, policy manuals, and contracted terms
  - reduce write-offs from denials
  - identify claims with higher likelihoods of clinical denial prior to submission
  - preventative workflows to assess and address claim gaps
  - align on clinical protocols in collaboration to improve individual and population health

- **Adoption / ROI / value-realization findings**
  - Technology deployments in RCM are often hampered by:
    - partial solutions “that fail to generate significant value because they never reach the minimum threshold for impact”
    - implementations that “don’t account for refining and customizing solutions, transitional periods, trial and error, or system downtime”
    - skills gaps spanning functions
    - competing challenges such as “operations under crisis (including the COVID-19 pandemic), electronic health-record implementation, and a rapidly evolving regulatory environment”
  - “Modest investments in proven technologies are now the norm and paradoxically prevent the realization of meaningful outcomes.”
  - “Many technology deployments purchase solutions for pilots without sufficiently considering their potential to eventually scale across the enterprise, which could cap the impact of the pilot.”
  - “the business case for the solution becomes more challenging when the potential investment is evaluated based only on its short-term value rather than the full potential of the new technologies to the organization”
  - Pilots for prior authorization “tend to fall short of stakeholders’ initial hopes, lack enterprise scalability, and limit sustainability of impact for the organization”
  - For denial-management pilots, “solutions may allow revenue cycle operators to work more efficiently by increasing the quantity and quality of claims processed”
  - Organizations focused only on “write-off value” may “decommission such a pilot quickly”
  - Those solutions can create value in the medium to longer term and also:
    - reduce unnecessary correspondence between payers and providers
    - improve staff experiences
    - reduce high volumes of work that can contribute to burnout
    - reduce the stress that denial of payment creates for patients

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors**
  - “top-team commitment to technology efforts, backed by a long-term vision”
  - “a holistic approach to investing in technology instead of one based on ad hoc funding of one-off experiments”
  - “a clear path to move offerings from pilot to systemwide adoption, with distinct deployments for pilots and full-scale implementation and tailored change management”
  - “a talent strategy that ensures technology efforts are led and supported by teams with experience in business, technology, and healthcare”
  - “holistic indicators of future value to measure success”
  - Leaders should “be nimble and failing fast when required, adjusting rapidly and pursuing opportunities for value as they shift, and investing for the long term”
  - “establish and model a willingness to seek out opportunities and a mindset of iteration and continuous improvement in rapid feedback cycles”
  - “open-ended assessment—and often, for maximal impact, redesign—of affected processes”
  - “coordination is key”
  - “Revenue cycle teams cannot shoulder an overhaul of their operations alone.”
  - “complex organizational structures make collaboration across departments necessary even when difficult”
  - “departments’ incentives” may need updating
  - understanding stakeholders’ journeys through a process and “the pain points along the way”
  - understanding where new technology and processes interface with legacy processes
  - technology should not be “dropped into entrenched tech environments, processes, and ways of working without accounting for the broader technology ecosystem”
  - “structure and streamline the system’s technology ecosystem, from vendors all the way down to health system data”
  - “Organizing the ecosystem in a structured way that is accessible and easy to navigate can help streamline new implementations, simplify data governance, reduce the risk of unexpected (or unknown) vendor capability duplication, and reduce potential errors across the system.”
  - “Deploying automation and analytics (and eventually, gen AI) works best in a setting where the talent involved has the time and expertise to be effective.”
  - “Cross-competency training is also helpful to unlock new opportunities to collaborate more effectively.”

- **Governance / risk obligations**
  - “establishing guardrails in how data are structured to minimize bias or inequitable impacts to different populations”
  - “having humans validate computer-generated outputs to prevent closed-loop automation”
  - “implement controls and protocols to prevent misuse and disuse”
  - “simplify data governance”
  - “reduce the risk of unexpected (or unknown) vendor capability duplication”
  - “risk-mitigation strategies” may reduce net economics, but break-even may still be acceptable if holistic value is created elsewhere
  - “new technologies such as gen AI come with risks”
  - “as with cybersecurity” implies cybersecurity-like controls are needed, but no further specifics are listed

- **Failure modes / reasons pilots and deployments underperform**
  - “partial solutions” that never reach “the minimum threshold for impact”
  - failure to account for “refining and customizing solutions, transitional periods, trial and error, or system downtime”
  - “skills gaps spanning functions”
  - “competing challenges” including COVID-19, electronic health-record implementation, and a rapidly evolving regulatory environment
  - “failure to improve the foundational infrastructure upon which technology depends”
  - “approaches to deployment and measurement that weigh on projects from the start”
  - “ad hoc funding of one-off experiments”
  - pilot-only purchasing without considering enterprise scale
  - evaluating solutions only on “short-term value”
  - stakeholders failing to:
    - update their tech stack and workflows
    - train staff to optimally use updated technology
    - redesign affected processes
  - dropped into “entrenched tech environments, processes, and ways of working”
  - technology ecosystem that is “messy, difficult to access, and difficult to navigate”
  - incentives and operational tradeoffs not updated across departments
  - “limited bandwidth for individuals and impeding collaboration critical for solution development”
  - projects assigned as an additional task to leaders who already have a full slate of responsibilities and only some expertise
  - technology talent shortages: “the United States has more open positions than candidates, especially in healthcare”

- **Specific examples / details**
  - Voice recognition dictation software is described as “Perhaps the most evocative use case in development”
  - It “records, transcribes, and structures notes from physician–patient encounters”
  - It “uses the information to complete administrative tasks in the background”
  - For denials, the article notes a shift from “simply managing denials” to preventing them
  - For bill submission tradeoff: an automation or gen AI solution may “decrease accounts receivable days” but “increase the average number of days it takes to submit a bill”
  - “This tradeoff may make the most sense for the organization because it ensures that documentation is accurate and comprehensive.”
  - Preventative claim workflows may require:
    - staff retraining to preemptively attach additional documentation
    - clinicians updating documentation approaches
    - payor contracting teams understanding operating model changes to improve collaboration with insurers
  - In the “most optimistic future,” payers and providers could “align on clinical protocols in collaboration to improve individual and population health”

- **Absence of requested information**
  - No formal ranking of use cases is provided on the page.
  - No explicit agentic AI term is used beyond gen AI and automation/analytics.
  - No vendor names, product names, or enterprise AI pipeline stages are specified.

title: Healthcare revenue cycle management under pressure | McKinsey
content:
- **Page relevance**
  - Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases because it contains explicit findings on:
    - AI and advanced technology priorities in revenue cycle management (RCM)
    - Automation functions/use cases
    - ROI expectations
    - Workflow and operating-model changes
    - Governance, vendor management, and adoption barriers
    - Failure modes in denials, appeals, and payer-related workflows

- **Research methodology / survey context**
  - “Now in its third year,” the **2025 McKinsey RCM Buyer’s Survey** was in the field from **September 19 to September 26, 2025**
  - It garnered responses from **215 US leaders** at care delivery organizations
  - The **2024 RCM Buyer’s Survey** was in the field from **October 23 to October 31, 2024**
  - The 2024 survey garnered responses from **293 US healthcare leaders** at care delivery organizations

- **Quantitative evidence relevant to AI / automation prioritization**
  - **51 percent** of leaders in the 2025 survey say **AI and advanced technologies are priority focus areas**
  - In the 2024 survey, **33 percent** of respondents said AI and advanced technologies were top priorities
  - The most prioritized functions in 2025 are:
    - **improving denial management and appeals (57 percent)**
    - **documentation and coding accuracy (56 percent)**
  - In 2024, “about half of respondents believed autonomous coding could manage over **35 percent** of outpatient coding volumes”
  - In 2025, “only a third of respondents believe **30 percent** of outpatient coding volume will be automated”
  - **8 percent** of the 2025 survey respondents expect **very high ROI** from automation
  - **42 percent** expect **high ROI over five years**
  - Compared with **18 percent** and **49 percent**, respectively, **over ten years**
  - **60 percent** of respondents say they plan to **change their vendor strategy over the next two years**
  - Only **6 percent** of respondents report plans to **reduce outsourcing due to technology**
  - **Half** of surveyed leaders note they plan to pursue **modular, integrated solutions**
  - **21 percent** say they expect to pursue **point solutions**

- **Quantitative evidence on financial pressure / operating impact**
  - “More than half” anticipate additional financial pressure from **H.R.1**
  - “Nearly half” note that the **cost to collect is rising**
  - More than **65 percent** of survey respondents anticipate **negative financial impacts due to H.R.1 alone**
  - Respondents foresee increases in:
    - **denial of payment (50 percent)**
    - **A/R days (56 percent)**
    - **self-pay bad debt and uncompensated care (76 percent)**
    - **share of out-of-pocket (85 percent)**
  - **47 percent** of respondents cite improving clinical denials as a top priority
  - Only **36 percent** report developing standardized processes
  - An average of **2.63 percent** of net patient service revenue (**NPSR**), weighted by response frequency, was written off due to clinical denials
  - Among respondents noting formal payer escalations were favorably resolved less than 60 percent of the time, cited obstacles include:
    - communication and coordination, such as extended review cycles or asynchronous communication with payers (**30 percent**)
    - authorization-related complexities, such as prior authorization and eligibility questions (**21 percent**)
    - coding-related discrepancies or differing interpretations of coding guidelines (**18 percent**)
  - A majority of respondents (**78 percent**) report that at least **10 percent of A/R lengthening** is attributable to payer-related causes
  - Escalated reimbursement issues took **36 days** to resolve on average
  - Only **43 percent** resulted in a favorable outcome for care delivery organizations
  - **45 percent** of respondents across organization sizes indicate that **cost to collect has been rising**

- **Named functions / use cases prioritized for automation**
  - “Improving denial management and appeals”
  - “Documentation and coding accuracy”
  - “Autonomous coding”
  - “Denials”
  - “A/R follow-up”
  - “Coding”
  - “Eligibility/authorization”
  - “Coding accuracy”
  - “Identify denial root causes”
  - “Automate A/R follow-up”
  - “Optimized documentation processes”
  - “Appeals automation”
  - “Payer engagement tools”
  - “Predict and mitigate the root causes of denials before appointments or billing”
  - “Underpayment recovery”
  - “Authorization optimization”
  - “Tools that surface contract misalignment or overlooked reimbursement”

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors explicitly stated**
  - “Deliberate governance”
  - “Domain-level transformation”
  - “Avoiding pilot purgatory”
  - “Phased transformation rather than an out-of-the-box solution”
  - “Establish ROI benchmarks”
  - “Prioritize credible, near-term (nine to 12 months) impact”
  - “Strengthen vendor governance”
  - “Well-defined service-level agreements”
  - “Recurring KPIs with leading and lagging indicators”
  - “Provisions for financial upside and downside risk sharing that align with regulatory requirements”
  - “Champion challenger” model:
    - “an incumbent solution is tested alongside a new-challenger solution in a live, low-risk environment before scaling the new solution”
  - “Joint operating committees with escalation infrastructure for payer engagement”
  - “Analytics-enabled insights into denial drivers”
  - “AI-enabled feedback loops can slow denial inflow and strengthen overturn rates”
  - “Automation reduces manual burden”
  - “Modular offerings can enable care delivery organizations to realize incremental value, validate performance, and scale capabilities over time”
  - “Derisked adoption models (such as invested pilots, performance-based pricing, and embedding AI within tech-enabled services)”

- **Adoption / vendor strategy findings**
  - Outsourcing strategies are shifting; **60 percent** plan to change their vendor strategy over the next two years
  - “Three-quarters” of that group planning to change outsourcing strategy intend to **expand their outsourcing efforts**
  - Respondents who say their organizations exceeded their RCM performance goals in the prior 12 months prefer:
    - expanding with existing vendors (**59 percent**)
    - versus new vendors (**41 percent**)
  - Those who indicate underperformance expect to expand through:
    - new vendors (**68 percent**)
    - versus existing vendors (**32 percent**)
  - Among respondents intending to bring RCM functions in-house, **75 percent** cite vendor performance management as a key need
  - Among those expanding within existing outsourced functions, **41 percent** cite vendor performance management as a key need
  - Among organizations likely to outsource, the top buying factors are:
    - maintaining operational control
    - ease of onboarding and implementation
    - pricing structure
  - For those planning to expand with existing vendors, the top priorities were:
    - interoperability
    - quality performance
    - breadth of capabilities

- **Failure modes / barriers / execution gaps**
  - “Execution gaps persist”
  - Appeal success for overturning denials remains low
  - “Net reimbursements increasingly falling below the cost of delivering care”
  - “Time to payment lengthening”
  - “Financial constraints”
  - “Interoperability challenges”
  - “Staff training”
  - “Change management”
  - “No single barrier (among seven assessed) exceeded 50 percent of responses”
  - “These four surpassed 40 percent”
  - “Many organizations still underinvest in denial prevention and instead rely primarily on downstream appeal management”
  - “Limited or ad hoc prevention resources”
  - “Varied staff across departments”
  - “Communication and coordination”
  - “Extended review cycles”
  - “Asynchronous communication with payers”
  - “Authorization-related complexities”
  - “Coding-related discrepancies or differing interpretations of coding guidelines”
  - “Pending medical records”
  - “Disputed claim authorizations”
  - “Appeal backlog”
  - “Pilot purgatory”
  - “Narrow point tools”
  - “Unfocused end-to-end offerings”
  - “Fragmented point solutions”

- **Governance / risk / compliance obligations explicitly stated**
  - “Stronger contract terms”
  - “Well-defined service-level agreements”
  - “Recurring KPIs with leading and lagging indicators”
  - “Provisions for financial upside and downside risk sharing that align with regulatory requirements”
  - “Regulatory mandates”
  - “New regulations stemming from H.R.1”
  - “Recent regulatory changes such as the No Surprises Act and hospital price transparency rules”
  - “Embedding regulatory intelligence into these workflows”
  - “Manage rising complexity and mitigate the potential downstream effects of new requirements, such as those in H.R.1”

- **Specific evidence by stakeholder group**

  | Stakeholder | Explicitly stated evidence |
  |---|---|
  | Care delivery organizations | Must “invest selectively while tightening operations as margins shrink”; “Prioritize automation with clear ROI”; “Strengthen vendor governance”; “Institutionalize denial prevention” |
  | Vendors | “Prove tangible ROI from AI”; “Align with care delivery organizations’ priorities”; “Reduce payer friction”; “Lead on denial prevention” |
  | Investors | “Back scalable modular solutions”; “Prioritize validated ROI”; “Invest in payer-facing capabilities” |

- **Additional exact findings and wording relevant to AI pipeline ranking**
  - “AI and automation in RCM is a priority, [but] leaders have more measured expectations for near-term returns”
  - “Current market dynamics favor scaled platforms that can integrate services and automation and build upon established capabilities within existing processes”
  - “Incumbents with strong performance and integrated platforms that can layer automation onto existing services and workflows may prove more favorable than introducing a new vendor—and workflow—into the operating environment”
  - “Surveyed leaders are favoring interoperable, multiworkflow platforms over fragmented point solutions”
  - “The market favors modular platforms that combine focused performance with scalable breadth to avoid both narrow point tools and unfocused end-to-end offerings”
  - “Vendors that can address root causes upstream while improving downstream overturn rates may find themselves better positioned than those focused solely on reactive denial management”
  - “Successful vendors will be those that act as intermediaries between payers and care delivery organizations, not just workflow enablers”

- **If using this page to rank enterprise AI pipeline use cases, the explicit use cases with strongest support on the page are**
  - Denial management and appeals
  - Documentation and coding accuracy
  - Autonomous coding
  - A/R follow-up
  - Denial root-cause identification
  - Appeals automation
  - Payer engagement tools
  - Predictive-denial prevention
  - Underpayment recovery

title: Why Software Companies' Customer Success Is Failing
content:
- **Page relevance**

- **Quantitative estimates / adoption / ROI findings**
  - “**Net revenue retention (NRR) rates**, a measure of how well companies retain and expand revenue from existing customers over a certain period, **decreased for 75% of software companies** in a recent Bain survey, **even as nearly 60% increased customer success spending**.”
  - “The share of **US enterprise software companies with a customer success team reached 60% this year, up from about 40% four years ago**, according to Bain analysis of LinkedIn and other data.”
  - “**nearly two-thirds of software customers feel their post-sales needs are only being moderately addressed or worse**.”
  - “Because emerging leaders apply the right resource to the right activity at the right time, **many have reduced spending while achieving better results**.”
  - “our analysis found that **companies with high NRR are much better than lower performers at cost-effectively deploying customer success resources**.”
  - “This improves efficiency while avoiding overly standardized activities that lose sight of the nuances of delivering value for individual customers with individual products.”
  - “Generative AI can be transformational in this arena, but only if the company has a well-defined product and customer journey blueprint.”

- **Named functions / use cases**

  - “ensuring that inefficiencies and existing problems aren’t automated (and thereby amplified).”
