title: Parsing How Winners Use AI
content:
- **Page relevance:** Relevant. The page discusses enterprise/B2B AI pipeline use cases, adoption, ROI/cost efficiency findings, workflow automation examples, governance/data foundation requirements, and failure modes.

- **Publication details**
  - Published on **April 23, 2025**
  - Part of **Bain's 2025 Commercial Excellence and Revenue Growth Agenda**

- **Adoption and scaling of AI**
  - **More than 90%** of about **1,300 commercial executives surveyed by Bain** have **scaled up at least one AI use case**.
  - **62%** of respondents said they have **scaled up to more than two use cases last year**.
  - **30%** of respondents said they have **scaled up to one to two use cases**.
  - AI deployment **met expectations for more than 90%** of respondents that have scaled up their use cases.
  - AI deployment **exceeded expectations for 57%** of respondents that have scaled up their use cases.
  - The article states that **nearly all companies have begun to deploy AI**.

- **Named functions / use cases**
  - **Knowledge management assistants**
    - Speed up **customization of materials for sales reps**.
  - **Identifying purchase intent among a long tail of buyers**
  - **Optimizing contracts**
  - **Customizing sales collateral**
  - **Customizing responses to requests for proposals**
    - IT services companies use AI to **stitch together critical technology capabilities and success stories from existing repositories**.
    - This can **speed up the process** and **showcase the applicable strengths and successes most relevant to particular customers**.
  - **Automated document preparation**
    - AI applied to **preparing requests for proposals in construction and manufacturing**.
    - Technology companies frequently use AI to **tailor sales materials for specific clients**.
  - **Automating sales rep tasks**
    - Can range from **helping reps enter the right details into their customer relationship management systems after each interaction**.
    - Can extend to **fully autonomous AI business development reps handling inbound or even outbound communications for initial sales stages**.
    - The latter typically applies to firms with **faster sales and lower ticket prices**.

- **Winner vs. laggard findings**
  - The article defines **winners** as companies that ranked **above the upper quartile of revenue growth for their sector and region in 2024** and demonstrated **positive gross margin growth**.
  - **Laggards** are companies that ranked **below the lower quartile of revenue growth for their industry and region in 2024**.
  - **Growth winners deploy more use cases—an average of 4.5 vs. just 3.3 for laggards.**
  - Winners are realizing **almost 2 times greater cost efficiencies** than laggards for any given use case.
  - Winners allocate **more resources to sales and marketing technologies broadly**, both:
    - **in absolute terms**
    - **as a proportion of their overall sales and marketing budget**

- **ROI / cost efficiency findings**
  - Companies following **four or more best practices** realize **12% cost efficiency**.
  - Companies following **none of the practices** realize **just 5%** cost efficiency.
  - Winners adhere to **three best practices on average vs. two for laggards**.

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors**
  - To make real progress requires a **systematic, measurable approach to AI deployment**.
  - Winners invest in managing the **changes required to make AI effective**.
  - Winners secure **senior executive sponsorship**.
  - Winners adhere to proven best practices, including:
    - **creating a robust business case**
    - **performing a buy vs. build evaluation**
    - **investing in training**
  - The article states that **technology and data foundations** are required to optimize AI.

- **Governance / risk / operational obligations**
  - **Slightly more than half of commercial organizations acknowledge that they have not set up adequate technology and data foundations to optimize AI**.
  - Main challenges include:
    - **incomplete or low-quality data**
    - **technology that’s not correctly configured**
  - **Incomplete or low-quality data**:
    - includes the **inability to create a unified customer profile**
    - usually stems from **poor data integration among different systems**
    - results in **duplicate or disconnected records**
  - **Poorly configured technology**:
    - occurs when organizations have **bought many different tools but fail to connect them**
    - makes the technology **less useful to end users**

- **Failure modes**
  - **Roughly a quarter of respondents’ sales and marketing AI pilots have failed**.
  - Among AI use cases in pilot phase, **roughly one-fifth are not meeting expectations**.
  - About **12% of respondents** said that their **AI deployment has not met expectations**.
  - **35% of laggards** that completed pilots on **automating sales representative tasks** are **no longer pursuing this capability**.

- **Additional stated conclusions**
  - **Using AI at scale has become table stakes for B2B companies**.
  - Growth prospects for the next few years hinge in part on deploying AI to **operate more efficiently** and **deliver better products and service to customers**.
description: High-growth firms invest more in the technology foundation to realize greater efficiencies and productivity from AI while low-growth firms lag.

title: The rise of authorized push payment fraud | Deloitte Insights
content:
- **Page relevance to enterprise AI pipeline use cases:**  
  - Relevant for **AI-driven fraud detection / fraud defense / risk monitoring** use cases in financial services.  
  - **Not primarily an enterprise AI pipeline use-case article**; it is a fraud-loss forecast article, but it contains explicit mentions of **generative AI**, **agentic AI**, **AI agents**, **real-time risk assessment**, and **autonomous decisions at speed and scale**.

- **Named AI-related functions / use cases explicitly stated**
  - **“generative AI and agentic AI”** used to:
    - create **highly realistic deepfake content**
    - **impersonate people**
    - **execute large-scale, targeted scams**
  - **“AI agents”** could transform fraud defense by:
    - **spotting anomalies**
    - **assessing risk in real time**
    - **monitoring transactions for anti-money laundering**
    - **making autonomous decisions at speed and scale**
  - The article also references **AI tools** in the context of fraudsters and financial institutions, but does not enumerate additional enterprise AI pipeline functions beyond the above.

- **Quantitative estimates / loss forecasts**
  - **$14.9 billion by 2028**: baseline scenario estimate for **authorized push payment fraud losses in the United States**
  - **$8.3 billion in 2024**: estimated U.S. APP fraud losses in the baseline scenario comparison point
  - **$18.2 billion by 2028**: aggressive scenario estimate, where **AI-driven APP fraud incidents outpace societal and institutional defenses**
  - **$4.6 billion in losses in 2024**: investment fraud losses
  - **surged over 14 times since 2020**: investment fraud growth
  - **$2.5 billion in APP fraud losses in 2024**: imposter scam losses
  - **$960 million in 2020**: imposter scam losses comparison point
  - **27% growth each year**: average growth rate for imposter scam losses
  - **360,487 cases**: business imposter scams in 2024
  - **212,267 reported cases**: government imposter scams in 2024
  - **$95 million in APP fraud losses** in tech support scams with victim’s reported age in 2024
  - **66%**: of those tech support scam losses were reported by **baby boomers (60 to 79 years)**
  - **19%**: of those tech support scam losses were reported by the **Silent Generation (above 80 years)**
  - **Over half** of victims of fraud (both authorized and unauthorized payments) consider switching financial providers
  - **30% actually do** switch financial providers
  - The 2024 study cited was of **10,000 consumers**

- **APP fraud types and ranking details**
  - **Investment fraud**:
    - tops the list among APP fraud types
    - **$4.6 billion** in losses in 2024
    - described tactic: **“pig butchering”**
  - **Imposter scams**:
    - rank just behind investment fraud in total losses
    - include fraudsters pretending to be:
      - a **romantic partner**
      - **bank or business**
      - **government agency**
      - **friend or family member**
      - **tech support**
    - **$2.5 billion** in losses in 2024
    - business imposter scams were the most reported type of APP fraud in 2024
  - The article says **investment scams are expected to account for the bulk of the growth in APP fraud losses, followed by bank and business impersonation and romance imposter scams.**

- **Adoption / ROI / institutional response findings**
  - **Banks in the United States aren’t legally required to reimburse customers for APP fraud**, though **some may in cases involving investment fraud**
  - Some US banks are responding with:
    - **payment verification steps**
    - **stronger education efforts**
  - The article states APP fraud may hurt customers’ **loyalty** to banking or payments institutions
  - The article says banks and payment institutions that help educate, remind, and work proactively with customers could benefit from **greater loyalty and trust**

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors explicitly stated**
  - AI agents could help by operating with:
    - **speed and scale**
    - **real time** risk assessment
    - **autonomous decisions**
  - Forecast assumptions were modeled around:
    - **AI adoption by both fraudsters and financial institutions**
    - **shifts in fraud frequency and success**
    - **the effectiveness of countermeasures**
    - **consumer awareness**
  - The article notes the rise of **real-time payment apps in the United States** increases the complexity for financial institutions to **quickly verify identity and stop fraud before funds are irreversibly transferred**
  - The article emphasizes **payment verification steps** and **stronger education efforts** as current defensive responses

- **Governance / risk / obligations explicitly stated**
  - **Unlike with unauthorized money transfers or credit card fraud, banks in the United States aren’t legally required to reimburse customers for APP fraud**
  - The article highlights anti-fraud measures used elsewhere:
    - **“confirmation of payee”** — an **industry-wide name-checking service** implemented in the **United Kingdom and Australia**
    - It **verifies recipient details before a transfer** by matching the **account name entered by the payer** with the **name on file at the recipient’s financial institution**
  - Cross-industry coordination is described as necessary because many scams originate through:
    - **telecom**
    - **social media platforms**
  - The **Aspen Institute’s National Task Force for Fraud and Scam Prevention**:
    - unites **33 cross-industry players**
    - includes **federal agencies**
    - **banks and payments institutions**
    - **tech platforms**
    - aims to tackle **consumer fraud**
  - The **bipartisan TRAPS Act**:
    - proposed in **June 2025**
    - aims to establish a **federal task force**
    - focused on combating **digital payment scams across consumer and commercial contexts**
  - **Stop Scams UK Unit**:
    - brings together **banks, telcos, tech firms, regulators, law enforcement, and consumer groups**
    - coordinates scam responses
    - runs awareness campaigns
    - shares fraud intelligence
  - **Australia pilot SMS Sender ID Registry**:
    - helps telecommunications companies block impersonation
    - does so by **verifying message headers from legitimate businesses**

- **Failure modes / risks / fraud mechanisms explicitly stated**
  - **Victims are tricked—often through social engineering—into authorizing payments themselves**
  - Transactions can become **almost impossible to reverse once the funds are gone**
  - Fraudsters use **layered deception**
  - Scams are becoming **more aggressive**
  - The playbook has **“n’t changed much—it’s just gotten more aggressive.”**
  - APP fraud is said to be **fast-growing**
  - Social engineering in APP fraud is poised to become **more sophisticated and difficult to detect**
  - The article says losses may be underestimated because:
    - **not all such scams are reported** to financial institutions or regulatory authorities like the **FTC or the FBI**
    - among reported cases, **information on the dollar amount of losses and the victims’ age is not shared in all cases**
    - one stated reason is **embarrassment**
  - It notes the method is complicated by **AI tools** available to fraudsters
  - It also notes that **real-time payment apps** make stopping fraud before transfer more difficult

- **Age / victim segment findings**
  - **Older adults are generally easier targets**
  - Older adults are **hardest hit by imposter scams**
  - For tech support scams, among cases with victim’s reported age in 2024:
    - **66%** were reported by **baby boomers (60 to 79 years)**
    - **19%** were reported by the **Silent Generation (above 80 years)**
  - Older adults are targeted because they:
    - tend to hold **more financial assets**
    - may be **less familiar with the evolving technologies scammers rely on**
  - Younger generations are disproportionately hit by:
    - **business and job opportunity scams**
    - **online shopping fraud**
    - **advance-fee credit traps**
  - The article states many young Americans are **digital natives** and frequently use **digital channels** to send and receive money

- **Methodology details explicitly stated**
  - Estimates are based exclusively on the **Federal Trade Commission’s Consumer Sentinel Network data from 2020 to 2024**
  - The dataset tracks **48 categories of reported fraud**
  - Deloitte focused on **20 fraud types** most vulnerable to APP fraud
  - The FTC data segmented fraud by **age group**, both in number of cases and dollar losses
  - Deloitte reclassified age groups into **five generational cohorts**:
    - **Gen Z**
    - **millennials**
    - **Gen X**
    - **baby boomers**
    - **the Silent Generation**
  - Each of the 20 categories was assigned an **APP fraud incidence rate (in percentage)**
  - Deloitte estimated the share of fraud within each category attributable to APP for every year from **2020 through 2024**
  - Not all fraud categories are susceptible to APP fraud, including:
    - **pyramid schemes**
    - **multi-level marketing**
    - **timeshare sales**
  - Deloitte modeled **three scenarios**:
    - **conservative**
    - **baseline**
    - **aggressive**
  - Forecast assumptions were grounded in **fraud typology analysis** and **validated with Deloitte specialists**

- **Named scams / tactics explicitly stated**
  - **“phantom hacker scams”**
  - **“pig butchering”**
  - **business imposter scams**
  - **government imposter scams**
  - **tech support scams**
  - **online shopping fraud**
  - **advance-fee credit traps**
  - **bank and business impersonation**
  - **romance imposter scams**
  - **investment scams**
  - **job opportunity scams**

- **If looking specifically for enterprise AI pipeline use cases**
  - The page does **not** provide a detailed enterprise AI pipeline, model ops, data pipeline, or agent orchestration framework.
  - It **does** explicitly mention AI-related fraud defense functions, AI-driven fraud growth, and forecasting assumptions involving AI adoption by fraudsters and financial institutions.
description: Deloitte estimates US losses from authorized push payment fraud could surge to nearly $15 billion by 2028. Who’s most vulnerable, and how can banks shore up their defenses?

title: From Prediction to Transformation
content:
- **Page relevance**
  - Relevant to ranking enterprise AI pipeline use cases because it discusses how AI prediction changes:
    - decision-making,
    - workflow design,
    - coordination vs. modularity,
    - value-chain ripple effects,
    - adoption patterns,
    - and system-level failure modes.

- **Core framing for AI value**
  - “AI has value only if it leads to better decision-making.”
  - “insights” is described as “precisely the wrong way to think about how an advance in AI will create value.”
  - “insights” often is code for “We don’t know what to do with our AI’s predictions.”
  - A “much better answer” is to describe “the decisions that the predictions will improve.”

- **Quantitative estimates and named statistics**
  - In **1960** just **6% of jobs** required core decision-making skills such as:
    - problem-solving,
    - diagnosing,
    - strategizing,
    - prioritizing.
  - By **2018** that number had reached **34%**.
  - “Two decades after Edison switched on the light bulb, only **3% of U.S. businesses used electricity**.”
  - In **1987**, Robert Solow said, “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.”
  - Verafin was acquired by Nasdaq for **$2.75 billion**.
  - In London, it takes **three to four years** for cabdrivers to learn all the city’s streets and the best routes through them.
  - In the America’s Cup example, after **eight weeks** the AI started to beat the sailors in the simulator.
  - Emirates Team New Zealand claimed the trophy, winning **seven races to three**.
  - The restaurant example uses:
    - **100 pounds every week** of avocados,
    - sometimes as little as **30 pounds**,
    - other weeks **300 pounds**.
  - The supplier example uses:
    - **25,000 pounds of avocados a week**,
    - fluctuating from **5,000 pounds to 50,000 pounds**.

- **Named functions / use cases / enterprise pipeline examples**
  - **Translation software**
    - Early AI application.
    - Predicts how people would translate a given text from one language to another based on how real humans have translated previous texts.
  - **AI classifying medical images**
    - Another early AI application.
    - Predicted what expert radiologists would say that scans showed.
  - **Financial fraud detection**
    - Verafin’s AI-driven technologies were used by hundreds of financial institutions as a substitute for security teams.
  - **Ride-sharing / navigation**
    - Internet-connected mobile phones allowed people to hail rides through an app and get navigation information cheaply.
    - AI on smartphones predicts the best routes, taking into account traffic conditions.
  - **Hiring / applicant screening**
    - AI helps HR decide what criteria to use to decide who gets an interview.
  - **Credit card verification**
    - Systems driven first by crude database checks and now by AI prediction automate approval decisions.
    - Purchases are approved according to rules set by a small group of people, most likely a committee.
  - **Medical imaging diagnosis**
    - AI-enabled diagnosis replaces radiologist judgment in the diagnostic step.
  - **Demand forecasting for restaurant inventory**
    - AI predicts what customers will choose.
    - Used to set order quantities for avocados.
  - **Amazon recommendation engine**
    - AI-based recommendation engine predicts the best product to suggest to a customer.
    - Amazon includes recommendations for products that are out of stock and will take longer to reach customers.

- **Adoption / ROI / value findings**
  - AI applications can have “enormous commercial value.”
  - Verafin’s fraud technologies were adopted by “hundreds of financial institutions.”
  - The adoption of AI in restaurant demand forecasting:
    - wastes less,
    - sells more,
    - and “Profitability rises.”
  - Emirates Team New Zealand:
    - AI sped up design iteration,
    - enabled better coordination between boat design and sailing maneuvers,
    - improved the learning process,
    - and helped the team win.
  - AI can enable “better and cheaper predictions than humans were making.”
  - AI can “slot into existing businesses without much fuss” in narrow-use cases.
  - AI can create value in isolated, tightly bounded applications first, and later broader transformation.

- **Workflow / agentic AI success factors**
  - AI should be built into “a system of decision-making,” not treated as “insights.”
  - Successful AI systems enable:
    - **coordination where possible**,
    - and **modularity where necessary**.
  - The adoption of AI “will often involve a system that finds an optimal balance of modularity and coordination.”
  - **Modularity**
    - “insulates decisions in one part of the organization from the variability—the ripple effects—that AI creates in others.”
    - “reduces the need for reliability.”
  - **Coordination**
    - “counters the lack of reliability that comes alongside AI adoption.”
    - is needed to align work and resources.
  - **Synchronization**
    - Example: rowers need to row in unison and adjust speed as the race progresses.
    - The coxswain is critical for gathering information, aggregating it, assessing the need for changes, and adjusting the message accordingly.
  - **Assignment problems**
    - Example: ambulance dispatching.
    - A central dispatcher, human or software, ensures only one ambulance responds.
    - The “wrong” ambulance is far less of a problem than sending none or too many.
  - **Amazon recommendation design**
    - Amazon recommends out-of-stock products and communicates likely delay to customers.
    - This balances learning with fulfillment.
    - The company has a “modular organization” that slots better AI predictions into recommendations while minimizing impact on the rest of the organization.
  - **System-level design**
    - “The complete system of the simulated boat and the AI sailor enabled improvements to both kinds of decisions.”
    - AI improved coordination between boat design and sailing maneuvers.

- **Decision-rights and organizational effects**
  - When predictions are extremely accurate, “decision rights will flow to where judgment is still needed.”
  - AI can change:
    - who makes decisions,
    - where decisions are made,
    - when decisions are made,
    - how decisions are made.
  - In ride-sharing:
    - vastly more people can be involved in making decisions about rides,
    - drivers’ control over decisions decreases.
  - In hiring:
    - AI concentrates decision-making without changing who has control.
    - One HR executive can decide what criteria to use to decide who gets an interview.
    - Fewer people are needed.
  - In credit card verification:
    - AI radically centralizes decision-making,
    - changing how and where it happens.
  - In medical imagery:
    - the physician becomes more important and powerful,
    - the radiologist less so.

- **Governance / risk obligations**
  - Credit card approval rules are set by “a small group of people, most likely a committee,” which “creates the risk parameters embedded in the programs that run verification devices.”
  - AI adoption can affect “your partners in the value chain and the ecosystem you operate in.”
  - “What works for you may create problems for them.”
  - In AI systems with coordination effects, “new communication systems may be required” to overcome them.
  - Communication may need to be designed to:
    - synchronize work,
    - assign resources,
    - communicate likely delays,
    - and coordinate decisions across organizations.
  - AI can create “ripple effects” across supply chains and ecosystems.

- **Failure modes / risks / limits**
  - AI can improve one person’s uncertainty while making “your own decisions become less reliable for others.”
  - The “fundamental problem—that demand needs to be aligned with supply—hasn’t really been solved.”
  - AI creates ripple effects that can force:
    - more unpredictability for suppliers,
    - more variability in supplier orders,
    - more fluctuation for upstream suppliers and growers.
  - Over-relying on local AI predictions without coordination can cause:
    - too much or too little inventory,
    - wasted product,
    - missed sales,
    - inability to supply enough avocados,
    - misalignment across the chain.
  - Communication alone is not always enough:
    - “A restaurant can’t create alignment along the supply chain through communication alone” because the chain spans “thousands of kilometers and many months.”
    - The investment would be “prohibitively expensive and time-consuming.”
  - In ride-sharing, if platforms did not exist, the taxi business might still be thriving.
  - In credit card verification, centralized rules can reject or approve based on programmed parameters rather than local human judgment.
  - Early AI applications are “hardly transformational” when they merely replace human prediction tasks without changing the rest of the business.
  - “The AI wasn’t handing Emirates Team New Zealand some insights.”
  - The article explicitly contrasts narrow applications with transformational system redesign.

- **Specific example details**
  - **America’s Cup / Emirates Team New Zealand**
    - Partnered with McKinsey.
    - Identified the main bottleneck to innovation: human sailors.
    - AI program was taught to sail using technology similar to AI that beat the world’s top players of Go.
    - The bot didn’t need to sleep or eat.
    - It could run thousands of simulations in the same time that it took the human crew to run just a handful.
    - The bot did “things that felt counterintuitive to the sailors,” and “they’d try them out on the water and they’d actually work.”
    - Previously, it could take weeks to figure out the best way to use a newly designed boat.
    - AI could experiment with multiple variations of the boat simultaneously, 24 hours a day.
    - It could try different racing tactics.
    - It sped up the cycle of design iteration and the development of new maneuvers.
    - The AI did not pilot the boat in the race; “the rules still require that real boats be piloted by real people.”
  - **Taxi / ride-sharing**
    - A platform eliminated the need for:
      - a mileage meter,
      - a method of taking payment,
      - a central dispatcher who assigns drivers to fill pickup requests.
    - Any driver with access to the platform can offer rides.
  - **Hiring**
    - Traditional hiring involved many HR people screening hundreds of résumés.
  - **Medical imaging**
    - Before AI prediction, physicians often called in expert radiologists for MRI, ultrasound, or X-ray.
    - With AI-enabled diagnosis replacing radiologist judgment, the physician’s own judgment becomes the only judgment involved in treatment decisions.
  - **Restaurant / supply chain**
    - Menu limits customer choices so the kitchen can make what they order.
    - AI demand forecasting changes weekly ordering quantities.
    - Local supplier and its suppliers experience more unpredictability.
    - Growers need to make crop-size decisions a year or more in advance.

- **Explicitly stated overall thesis**
  - AI’s promise is similar to electricity and personal computing.
  - AI began by resolving a few immediate problems in isolated applications.
  - As people engage with AI, they will spot new opportunities for creating solutions or improving efficiency and productivity.
  - As AI spreads across supply chains and ecosystems, “all the processes and practices we took for granted are being transformed—not by the technology itself but by the creativity of the people who are using it.”
description: While the popular view is that insights are the key benefit of artificial intelligence, in truth AI creates value by improving the quality of decisions. The good news is, the opportunities for it to do that in business are countless. But because decisions in one area of an organization usually have an impact on decisions in other areas, introducing AI often entails redesigning whole systems. In that way, AI is similar to groundbreaking technologies of the past, like electricity, which initially was used only narrowly but ultimately transformed manufacturing. Decisions involve a combination of prediction and judgment, and because AI makes highly accurate predictions, it will shift decision rights to where judgment is still needed, potentially changing who makes decisions and where, when, and how. More-accurate predictions in one part of a value chain will also have ripple effects on other parts. For instance, if a restaurant can reliably forecast the amount of ingredients it needs each week, its orders will fluctuate, making its suppliers’ sales more uncertain. Strong communication is needed to synchronize effort and resources in a system, and modularity will help prevent changes in one area from disrupting others.
